Newborns born to adolescents aged <18 (PB adjusted odds ratio [aOR]= 1.25, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.11-1.41; NICU aOR= 1.19, 95% CI: 1.06-1.33; PD aOR= 1.33, 95% CI: 0.99-1.80) and 18-19 years (PB aOR= 1.04, 95% CI: 0.98-1.11; NICU aOR= 1.08, 95% CI: 1.01-1.16; PD aOR= 1.17, 95% CI: 0.98-1.40) had higher odds for almost all the selected perinatal outcomes than newborns born to the reference group of 20-29-year-old women. If adolescents <20 years had postponed childbirth until they were between 20 and 29 years old, approximately 14 cases of singleton preterm birth (1%), 16 NICU admissions (1%), and 4 perinatal deaths (2%) occurring between 2017 and 2022 could have been prevented.
CONCLUSION: Our findings revealed large geographical differences in adolescent births across Georgia, with the highest rates in Kvemo Kartli, Kakheti, and Imereti. Adolescent childbirth, particularly among those <18 years, was linked to higher risks of PB, NICU admission, and PD compared to adults aged 20-29 years. Targeted interventions, such as improved access to reproductive health education and family planning, are needed, especially in high-burden regions.

articles.title: Maintaining integrity amidst turmoil: A qualitative exploration of parental coping process during hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for pediatric cancer.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Childhood cancer, particularly pediatric hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), imposes profound psychosocial and socioeconomic challenges on parents. This study aimed to develop a grounded theory explaining the dynamic coping process experienced by parents during their child's HSCT journey.
METHODS: This qualitative study used Corbin and Strauss's (2015) grounded theory approach to develop an explanatory account of the parental coping process during pediatric HSCT. Twenty Persian-speaking parents of children undergoing HSCT at a tertiary care center in Iran were recruited through purposive and theoretical sampling. Data collection began with unstructured interviews and progressed to in-depth semi-structured interviews. Data were analyzed through constant comparative analysis, including open, axial, and selective coding.
RESULTS: Parental coping during pediatric HSCT was a multifaceted, non-linear process shaped by evolving stressors and adaptive responses. The analysis generated a grounded theory centered on the core category, "maintaining integrity amidst turmoil," which reflected parents' efforts to manage their central concern, "entrapment in adversity," arising from perceived threats and trapped in suffering. Coping was mediated through two key strategies: "health-seeking behaviors" and "emotional and cognitive coping efforts". Contextual factors, including a "continuum of support systems" (ranging from empowering healthcare interactions to systemic inadequacies) and "beliefs and individual situation" (cultural, spiritual, and personal values), significantly influenced coping trajectories. Outcomes included "relative adaptation" and "self-actualization".
CONCLUSIONS: Tailored support systems that address systemic gaps and cultural beliefs are essential for fostering adaptive coping. Strengthening health-seeking and emotional-cognitive strategies can promote functional stability and personal growth among parents.

articles.title: Association between active helicobacter pylori infection and Iron Deficiency Anemia among pregnant women attending antenatal care in Uganda: An analytical cross-sectional study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Helicobacter pylori infection has been associated with iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) during pregnancy, but evidence from Uganda remains limited. This study compared IDA prevalence by H. pylori status, assessed the adjusted association between H. pylori positivity and IDA, and explored factors associated with IDA among infected pregnant women.
METHODS: A facility-based analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among 392 pregnant women attending antenatal care at Mubende Regional Referral Hospital, Uganda, from August to December 2025. Participants were systematically recruited into H. pylori-positive and -negative analytical groups (196 each). Active H. pylori infection was determined using stool antigen testing, and IDA was defined by concurrent anaemia and serum ferritin <15 µg/L. Prevalence ratios (PRs) were estimated for the H. pylori-IDA association, while logistic regression explored factors associated with IDA among H. pylori-positive women.
RESULTS: IDA was more prevalent among H. pylori-positive than -negative women (14.8% [29/196] vs 6.6% [13/196]). H. pylori positivity was associated with a higher prevalence of IDA (cPR = 2.23, 95% CI: 1.20-4.16; p = 0.012), including after adjustment for residence, iron-rich food consumption and household income (aPR = 2.22, 95% CI: 1.16-4.24; p = 0.016). Median haemoglobin was lower among H. pylori-positive women (11 vs 12 g/dL; p < 0.001). Among H. pylori-positive women, lack of deworming (aOR=4.88, 95% CI: 1.73-13.79), tea or coffee consumption with meals (aOR=4.31, 95% CI: 1.22-15.20), and inadequate handwashing (aOR=3.18, 95% CI: 1.15-8.76) were associated with higher odds of IDA.
CONCLUSIONS: H. pylori positivity was associated with a higher prevalence of IDA among pregnant women attending ANC at Mubende Regional Referral Hospital. Lack of deworming, tea or coffee consumption with meals, and inadequate handwashing were associated with IDA among H. pylori-positive women. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and the subgroup findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the limited number of IDA cases.

articles.title: Untargeted plasma metabolomics reveals metabolite alterations and pathway perturbations in gestational diabetes mellitus.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is defined as glucose intolerance first detected during pregnancy and is associated with adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. Metabolomics provides a system-level approach to characterize metabolic alterations associated with gestational insulin resistance. This study aimed to identify plasma metabolite differences between women with GDM and normal glucose tolerance (NGT) and to evaluate the discriminatory performance of a metabolite-based panel.
METHODS: Plasma samples from 270 pregnant women (169 GDM and 101 NGT) were analyzed using an untargeted 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR)-based metabolomics approach. Differential metabolites were identified using univariate, followed by multivariate modeling and regression adjustment for maternal age and pre-pregnancy body mass index. Discriminatory performance was evaluated using Random Forest (RF), Partial Least Squares-Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA), and Linear Support Vector Machine (Linear-SVM) models with Receiver Operating Characteristic curve analysis. Pathway enrichment analyses were performed using KEGG and SMPDB, and disease-based enrichment was assessed using HMDB.
RESULTS: Among 31 identified metabolites, 14 differed significantly between GDM and NGT. Integration of univariate and multivariate analyses prioritized nine metabolites-acetone, citrate, glucose, succinate, glycine, 3-hydroxybutyrate, leucine, phenylalanine, and the CH = CH bond of unsaturated lipids-that remained independently associated with GDM after covariate adjustment. All nine metabolites were elevated in the GDM group. A nine-metabolite panel achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.76 (95% CI: 0.70-0.81) using the RF model. Pathway enrichment identified valine, leucine, and isoleucine biosynthesis and ketone body metabolism as significantly enriched pathways. HMDB-based disease enrichment showed overlap with preeclampsia-related metabolic signatures.
CONCLUSION: Untargeted 1H NMR metabolomics, combined enrichment analyses, identified coordinated metabolic disturbances in GDM involving amino acid and ketone body metabolism. A nine-metabolite panel demonstrated moderate discriminative performance and provides mechanistic insight into GDM-associated metabolic adaptations, supporting their potential utility for future biomarker validation and translational studies.

articles.title: Clinical features, first aid practices, and hospital management of snakebites in Northern Uganda: A multi-facility cross-sectional study.
articles.abstract: Snakebite envenoming is a neglected tropical disease with a disproportionate burden in sub-Saharan Africa, where weak surveillance, limited antivenom availability, and reliance on traditional remedies compound morbidity and mortality. Evidence on how snakebite cases are clinically managed in routine practice in Uganda remains scarce. We conducted a facility-based cross-sectional study with retrospective abstraction of records from four purposively selected health facilities in Gulu and Arua Districts of Northern Uganda. Snakebite case records from outpatient, inpatient, paediatric, and intensive-care service points covering the period 2017-2021 were reviewed using a standardised abstraction tool. Descriptive statistics were computed in Stata version 14, with frequencies and proportions for categorical variables and medians with interquartile ranges (IQR) for continuous variables, both of which were right-skewed. All analyses were complete-case, and the denominator is reported wherever it differs from the full sample. We analysed 227 snakebite case records. Of these, 58.6% were female and the median age was 21 years (IQR 13-38); students or pupils accounted for 26.6% of the 192 records in which occupation was described. Most bites involved the lower limb (85.9%) and occurred in the second and third quarters of the year (59.9%). Snake species was undocumented in 76.2% of records. No pre-hospital first aid was recorded in 59.1% of cases; where first aid was documented it was usually harmful, most often a tourniquet (29.3%) or a herbal remedy (8.9%). The dominant clinical manifestations were pain (60.8%), swelling or blisters at the bite site (68.7%), and fang marks (26.9%). One or more features suggestive of systemic envenoming were documented in 18.5% of cases, of whom 33.3% received antivenom. Overall, only 15.0% of cases received antivenom, while supportive care predominated (intravenous fluids 68.1%, analgesics 64.2%, antibiotics 53.1%). Coagulation testing was rare (20-minute whole blood clotting test 17.3%; INR 12.0%). Overall, 93.4% of patients recovered, 3.1% died, 0.9% were referred to other healthcare facilities, and the rest (2.6%) had missing information on the outcomes. Snakebite management in Northern Uganda is largely symptomatic, with critical gaps in species identification, syndromic assessment, coagulation testing, antivenom utilisation, and pre-hospital first aid practices. Strengthening health-worker training, improving documentation and surveillance, and community education on appropriate first aid are urgently needed to reduce preventable morbidity and mortality.

articles.title: Sensorimotor representation in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis compared with healthy controls: Proprioception, tactile acuity, left-right judgment, and motor imagery.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is increasingly recognized as involving central sensorimotor alterations beyond structural spinal deformity, yet multiple sensorimotor domains have not been assessed comprehensively within a single AIS sample. This study aimed to compare tactile acuity, proprioception, left/right judgment, and motor imagery between adolescents with AIS and healthy controls, and to explore the associations of these sensorimotor domains with postural, body image, and health-related quality-of-life outcomes.
METHODS: In this cross-sectional case-control study, 41 adolescents with AIS and 42 healthy controls were assessed for tactile acuity, proprioception, left/right judgment, motor imagery, and pressure pain threshold, alongside body image, perceived spinal appearance, and quality of life.
RESULTS: Adolescents with AIS showed elevated paraspinal two-point discrimination thresholds at right T10, right L4, and left L4 (all adjusted p ≤ 0.040), but not at left T10, greater spinal repositioning errors in all four tested directions (all adjusted p ≤ 0.005), and poorer external visual motor imagery (adjusted p = 0.023). No between-group differences were found for left/right judgment or pressure pain threshold (all adjusted p > 0.05). Proprioceptive measures showed the strongest discriminative ability (lumbar right lateral flexion and lumbar flexion repositioning errors: AUC = 0.802 and 0.794, both p < 0.001), and a three-variable exploratory model correctly classified 82.9% of participants in the original sample and 81.7% after leave-one-out cross-validation. Body image disturbance and perceived spinal appearance were also worse in the AIS group, as were SRS-22 function, self-image, and subtotal scores (all adjusted p ≤ 0.012).
CONCLUSION: Adolescents with AIS showed impairments in tactile acuity, proprioception, and external visual motor imagery relative to healthy controls. These cross-sectional findings suggest that sensorimotor alterations may be relevant when designing rehabilitation strategies for this population, but they should be interpreted cautiously and do not establish causality. Larger longitudinal and neuroimaging-based studies are needed to clarify these relationships.

articles.title: Developing a syndromic case definition for timely surveillance of severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) based on financial claim codes in the Netherlands.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: To improve pandemic preparedness, a sustainable and timely surveillance system for severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) is crucial. We developed and evaluated a proxy for syndromic SARI-surveillance using financial claim codes (DTC-codes).
METHODS: With data from 2016-2020 we compared DTC-codes with primary discharge diagnosis classified by ICD-10 codes (J0-J22, U07) as comparative benchmark for SARI, distinguishing between paediatric and adult populations, and pre- and during COVID-19-pandemic periods. To establish DTC-based proxies for SARI, accuracy metrics of individual and combinations of DTC-codes, and temporal trends were assessed. We retrospectively assessed its ability to detect COVID-19 epidemic patterns and its relationship with outcomes of existing respiratory surveillance systems.
RESULTS: For adults, DTC-codes for pneumonia and unspecified respiratory and viral infections served as proxy for SARI. In the paediatric population, codes for laryngitis subglottica, RSV bronchiolitis and respiratory tract infection were used. While trends in DTC-based SARI proxies correlate with trends in ICD-10-coded SARI, the accuracy relative to this benchmark was moderate. The adult DTC-based SARI proxy reflected peaks in COVID-19 hospitalisations during the pandemic and aligned with influenza and RSV laboratory detections in the pre-pandemic period. The paediatric DTC-based SARI proxy aligned with RSV laboratory detections.
CONCLUSION: We established DTC-based proxies for syndromic SARI-surveillance that appeared suitable to monitor SARI-trends. However, on the patient level the accuracy for ICD-10-coded SARI appeared moderate. Accuracy of the DTC-based SARI proxy and its ability to detect relevant epidemic signals, should be assessed prospectively with real-time data.

articles.title: Misinformation-based preventive behaviors during the COVID-19 pandemic in Myanmar: A cross-sectional study.
articles.abstract: Widespread misinformation influenced public understanding of disease risk and preventive behaviors during the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly in low-resource and conflict-affected settings such as Myanmar. Although preventive behaviors were generally protective, some actions driven by misinformation may have been ineffective or harmful. Evidence on determinants of misinformation-based preventive behaviors remained limited. This study aimed to examine associations between misinformation-based preventive behaviors (MPB) and sociodemographic characteristics, information sources, social media use, and health belief factors in Myanmar. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among adults residing in Myanmar, with data collected between March and May 2024. Participants were asked to retrospectively report their preventive behaviors during the COVID-19 pandemic period (2020-2022). Data were collected using a structured questionnaire adapted from previous COVID-19 studies. The outcome variable was misinformation-based preventive behaviors, categorized as low (0-2 behaviors) and high (3-4 behaviors) engagement. Independent variables included sociodemographic characteristics, information sources, social media platform use, and selected health belief variables based on the Health Belief Model (HBM). A total of 434 respondents were included in the analysis, of whom 106 (24.4%) reported high engagement in MPB. Use of social media platforms other than Facebook was associated with higher engagement (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 2.30, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.22-4.35). Participants reporting ≤3 hours and 4-6 hours of daily social media use had lower odds of MPB engagement compared with those reporting >6 hours (AOR = 0.46, 95% CI: 0.25-0.86; AOR = 0.48, 95% CI: 0.24-0.95, respectively). Higher self-efficacy was independently associated with greater engagement in MPB (AOR = 1.70, 95% CI: 1.03-2.82). MPB were more strongly associated with information environments and specific health beliefs than with sociodemographic characteristics alone. These findings underscore the importance of addressing misinformation and improving access to reliable health information to reduce engagement in non-evidence-based practices.

articles.title: Knowledge, attitudes, and practices of Jordanian mothers regarding acute gastroenteritis in children.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: This study aimed to evaluate the knowledge, attitudes, and reported practices of mothers living in Jordan regarding childhood acute gastroenteritis and to identify factors associated with poor knowledge, poor practice, lack of oral rehydration solution (ORS) awareness, and antibiotic use without medical consultation.
METHODS: An analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among 730 mothers living in Jordan using a structured Arabic-language questionnaire. Participants were recruited through paediatric hospital settings and social media using convenience sampling. Composite knowledge and practice scores were calculated, and four multivariable binary logistic-regression models were fitted to examine factors associated with the prespecified outcomes.
RESULTS: The mean composite knowledge score was 15.73 ± 6.83 out of 28, corresponding to 56.18% of the maximum score, and 31.37% of participants were categorized as having poor knowledge. The mean composite practice score was 4.58 ± 1.71 out of 10, corresponding to 45.84% of the maximum score, and 61.23% were categorized as having poor practice. Overall, 54.52% identified three or fewer of the eight dehydration signs assessed, 59.59% were aware of ORS, and 3.15% selected ORS as their intended first action. Compared with residence in Central Jordan, residence in North Jordan was associated with higher adjusted odds of poor knowledge (aOR 2.18, 95% CI 1.38-3.45), poor practice (aOR 1.74, 95% CI 1.19-2.55), lack of ORS awareness (aOR 1.52, 95% CI 1.01-2.28), and antibiotic use without medical consultation (aOR 1.81, 95% CI 1.12-2.91). University-level education was associated with lower odds of poor knowledge and poor practice, while healthcare employment was associated with lower odds of poor practice and lack of ORS awareness.
CONCLUSION: Important gaps were identified in dehydration-sign recognition, ORS-related intended practices, and overall reported home-management practices. These findings support the development and evaluation of targeted caregiver-education initiatives emphasizing dehydration recognition, appropriate ORS use, safe medication practices, and timely care-seeking. Regional and educational differences may help identify groups requiring additional support; however, the observed associations should not be interpreted causally because of the cross-sectional design.

articles.title: Neurodevelopment among children under five years with sickle cell disease in Eastern Uganda: A propensity score analysis.
articles.abstract:
AIM: We compared neurodevelopment among children under-five years with and without sickle cell disease in eastern Uganda.
METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study between March and September 2025 at the pediatric sickle cell clinic of Mbale Regional Referral Hospital. We included 350 children under five years (117 with sickle cell disease and 233 without sickle cell disease). The primary outcome was neurodevelopment assessed using the Malawi Development Assessment Tool. We performed independent sample t-tests to compare development for age z-scores between children with and without sickle cell disease. We used inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses to calculate the effect of sickle cell disease on neurodevelopment.
RESULTS: The median age of the children was 40.9 months (interquartile range 27.8 to 54.3 months). Children with sickle cell disease had 0.89 lower DAZ scores compared to their peers without sickle cell disease. Among the children with sickle cell disease, those not enrolled on hydroxyurea had 0.4 lower DAZ scores in the social and language domains compared to those on hydroxyurea. The average exposure effect, obtained from the inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses, was -0.87, 95% CI [-1.19, -0.55] and the average exposure effect among the exposed was - 0.62 95% CI [- 1.01, - 0.23].
CONCLUSION: Children with sickle cell disease had lower developmental scores across all domains (social, gross motor, fine motor and language) compared to community controls. These findings highlight the developmental vulnerability associated with sickle cell disease in early childhood. Efforts towards timely screening and management of developmental delays among children are needed to improve their quality of life and long-term development. This may be through integration of neurodevelopmental screening into routine sickle cell disease care.

articles.title: Population-level associations of interpersonal trauma during childhood and adulthood with mental health and addiction problems.
articles.abstract: Interpersonal trauma during childhood and adulthood is associated with many adverse mental health and addiction outcomes. However, methodological issues of previous studies make it difficult to estimate and compare these associations at the population level. The objective of this study was to estimate and compare associations of self-reported interpersonal trauma during childhood and adulthood with several adverse mental health and addiction-related outcomes using population-based data. Using general population survey data among adults aged 18 + years (n = 4,016), we conducted logistic regression analyses to estimate the association between interpersonal trauma (never, childhood only, adulthood only, childhood and adulthood) and seven outcomes including psychological distress, suicidal ideation, ADHD symptoms, hazardous drinking, daily cannabis use, problematic electronic device use, and problem gambling. We also estimated population attributable fractions for any lifetime trauma in the seven outcomes. Overall, 18.3% of adults reported interpersonal trauma (9.2% childhood only, 5.0% adulthood only, and 4.1% both childhood and adulthood). In our main models, interpersonal trauma was significantly associated with psychological distress, suicidal ideation, ADHD symptoms, hazardous drinking, daily cannabis use, and problematic electronic device use, but not problem gambling. There was no evidence of interaction between childhood trauma and adulthood trauma for any of the outcomes either on the multiplicative or additive scale. Population attributable fraction estimates of lifetime trauma were significant for all seven outcomes ranging from 5.5% to 12.4%. Interpersonal trauma during either childhood or adulthood is strongly associated with, and may account for a significant proportion of, mental health and addiction problems at the population level. Based on current evidence, policymakers should place a higher priority on developing prevention strategies for interpersonal trauma to reduce the burden of mental health and addiction problems.

articles.title: Latent profiles of parental discipline in Singapore: Intergenerational patterns and links to adjustment in young adulthood.
articles.abstract: Using a person-centered approach, this paper examined parental discipline profiles in Singapore from parents' and young adults' perspectives, and how these were linked to young adults' adjustment. Two quantitative studies were conducted to explore parents' experiences of disciplining their children (Study 1) and young adults' experiences of receiving discipline (Study 2). Study 1 utilized the self-reported ISPCAN Child Abuse Screening Tool for Parents (ICAST-P) to document the frequency of use of 36 discipline methods. The ICAST-P was reworded for Study 2 to assess young adults' experiences of being disciplined. Latent class analysis identified three groups of disciplinarians in each study. Study 1 (N = 747 parents; 80.7% mothers) showed that 14.6% of participants were harsh disciplinarians (high psychological-physical/violent discipline), 54.5% were high psychological-low physical/violent disciplinarians, and 30.8% were low psychological-physical/violent disciplinarians. Parents who endorsed physical discipline and had been physically punished during childhood were more likely to be harsh disciplinarians. Study 2 (N = 667; 74.3% females; age 18-25) showed three similar groups: harsh disciplinarians (4.0% mothers; 6.1% fathers), the high psychological-moderate physical/violent discipline group (34.0% mothers; 37.7% fathers), and the moderate psychological-low physical/violent discipline group (62.0% mothers; 56.1% fathers). Young adults whose parents used moderate psychological and low levels of physical/violent discipline had the least emotion dysregulation, the best parent-child relationship, and the highest self-esteem. The potential long-term impact of harsh discipline and intergenerational transmission of harsh discipline are discussed.

articles.title: Beyond generalizations: Understanding adolescent social networks in American Indian communities.
articles.abstract: American Indian (AI) adolescents experience disproportionately high rates of substance use, yet the role of substance use and other individual characteristics in friendship network formation within AI-majority reservation schools remains understudied. Most existing research on adolescent networks derives from racially heterogeneous school settings, where substance use is often linked to friendship formation and popularity. This study examines the structural and relational foundations of friendship networks among AI adolescents in their unique cultural context. Using social network data from 9th and 10th-grade students (N = 247) across three schools on a Northern Plains reservation, we employed exponential random graph models (ERGMs) to analyze factors shaping friendship ties. Models assessed endogenous structural processes (reciprocity, transitivity, degree effects) and actor-level characteristics, including demographic factors, substance use (alcohol, tobacco, marijuana), depression, and AI identity. Results indicated that universal structural mechanisms (reciprocity, transitivity) and demographic homophily (gender, grade, sexual orientation) were primary drivers of friendship. However, unlike what is often observed in studies of other adolescent populations, substance use showed no consistent association with sending ties or receiving ties. Similarly, depression and AI identity were not substantively associated with friendship formation. These findings reveal a distinct relational ecology within AI-majority reservation schools, where peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors. These findings challenge assumptions underpinning many network-based prevention programs and underscore the critical need for theories and interventions that are culturally and contextually grounded in the lived experiences of AI youth.

articles.title: Prevalence and associated factors of influenza A virus infection among patients with acute respiratory tract infections in Gondar City, Northwest Ethiopia.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Influenza A virus is a major cause of acute respiratory tract infections and contributes substantially to the global disease burden. Laboratory-confirmed data on influenza A virus infection remain limited in the study area. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the prevalence of influenza A virus infection and to identify possible associated factors among patients with acute respiratory tract infections attending selected health institutions in Gondar City, Northwest Ethiopia.
METHODS: A multi-center, health facility-based cross-sectional study was carried out from January 1, 2025 to December 31, 2025. In total, 490 patients with acute respiratory tract infections were enrolled from five health facilities in Gondar City. Demographic, behavioral, and clinical information was collected using a structured questionnaire. Nasopharyngeal swabs were collected and tested for influenza A virus using multiplex real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with influenza A virus infection.
RESULTS: Influenza A virus was detected in 65 of the 490 participants, with an overall prevalence of 13.3% (95% CI: 10.3-16.3). Among the confirmed cases, 48 (73.8%) were A(H1N1) and 17 (26.2%) were A(H3N2). In multivariable logistic regression, participants aged 5-17 years (AOR: 3.14; 95% CI: 1.36-7.25; p = 0.008) and 18-49 years (AOR: 3.50; 95% CI: 1.54-7.20; p = 0.002) had higher odds of infection than those aged <5 years. Secondary education was associated with lower odds of infection compared with no formal education (AOR: 0.07; 95% CI: 0.01-0.75; p = 0.029), while employed participants had higher odds than students (AOR: 3.54; 95% CI: 1.47-7.80; p = 0.028).
CONCLUSION: Influenza A virus infection was detected among patients presenting with acute respiratory tract infections in Gondar City, highlighting the importance of influenza surveillance and laboratory confirmation in this population. Strengthening routine molecular surveillance, promoting seasonal influenza vaccination among high-risk populations, reinforcing infection prevention and control measures, and implementing targeted community health education are essential to improve influenza prevention and control.

articles.title: Age as a determinant of trampoline-related oral-facial-head injuries in pediatric emergency department visits: A NEISS analysis.
articles.abstract: Over the last decade trampoline use has increased. Many injuries occur that require emergency department (ED) care. The purpose of this research is to examine the role of age in trampoline-related oral-facial-head injuries that require ED care. Data from the 2024 National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) was used. Trampoline-related injuries were extracted from the data set. Oral-facial-head trampoline-related injuries were compared with other types of trampoline-related injuries by age groups (0 to <6 years, 6 to <12 years, and 12 to ≤18 years) in Chi-Square analyses and logistic regression analyses. There were 3548 NEISS-reported trampoline-associated injuries for children, ages 0 to ≤18 years, in 2024. This corresponded to an estimated 101,474 trampoline injuries in the United States in 2024. Of these, 21.7% were oral-facial-head trampoline-related injuries (weighted estimate of 22,033 injuries). Of all the trampoline-related injuries in children ages 0 to ≤18 years, children ages 0 to <6 years had 33.0% of the injuries; children ages 6 to <12 years had 51.9%; and, children ages 12 to ≤18 years had 15.1%. Children ages 0 to <6 years had an adjusted odds ratio of 1.66 [95% CI: 1.11, 2.50; p = 0.0155] compared with children ages 12 to ≤18 years for oral-facial-head trampoline-related injuries as compared with other injuries from trampolines. Younger children have significantly higher odds of trampoline-related oral-facial-head injuries requiring emergency department care compared with adolescents, supporting age as an important host factor within the Haddon Matrix framework. These findings highlight the need for targeted prevention and anticipatory guidance for younger children.

articles.title: Development and internal validation of VA-BLED for 1-year esophageal variceal bleeding risk in cirrhosis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Esophageal variceal bleeding is a life-threatening complication of cirrhosis, yet current risk stratification targets portal hypertension stage and endoscopic stigmata instead of short-term bleeding probability. We evaluated whether a simple score built from routinely available variables could stratify 1-year esophageal variceal bleeding risk.
METHODS: We developed and internally validated two multivariable logistic models in a retrospective outcome-balanced cohort of 108 patients with esophageal varices (54 variceal bleeding, 54 no bleeding). VA-BLED BASE incorporated Child-Pugh score, normalized alanine aminotransferase, and current alcohol use. VA-BLED HISTORY additionally incorporated previous bleeding. Performance was assessed from out-of-fold predictions using discrimination, calibration, and decision curve analysis.
RESULTS: VA-BLED BASE achieved an out-of-fold area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.732 (95% confidence interval, 0.635-0.827), which increased to 0.798 (95% confidence interval, 0.705-0.883) when previous bleeding history was included. Both models provided net benefit across clinically plausible threshold probabilities. At an assumed annual bleeding prevalence of 10%, VA-BLED BASE generated low-, intermediate-, and high-risk zones, whereas VA-BLED HISTORY functioned primarily as a high-risk enrichment model.
CONCLUSIONS: In this proof-of-concept development study, VA-BLED BASE and VA-BLED HISTORY stratified 1-year EVB risk using routinely available clinical variables and identified subgroups enriched for bleeding events. External validation in cohort-design populations is required before clinical application.

articles.title: Prosthetist perspectives for the rehabilitation of children with lower limb loss: A qualitative exploration in Cambodia.
articles.abstract: Rehabilitation for children with lower limb absence presents a multifaceted challenge due to their physical and cognitive development. Prosthetists have specialised expertise in this area, but despite significant involvement in adult research, their engagement in paediatric research remains limited. This limits knowledge dissemination across the sector, especially for those facing an influx of paediatric patients such as in humanitarian settings. This study aimed to capture prosthetists' expertise across the care pathway to achieve successful prosthetic limb fitting for children with lower limb absence in Cambodia. Structured interviews were conducted and analysed thematically, identifying six themes: 1) Starting rehabilitation with service awareness to maximise attendance using community outreach and proactive follow-up appointments; 2) multidisciplinary teamwork extending beyond specialised clinicians to include the child and their family, and empathetic communication, which often relied on parents as children may have difficulty articulating their needs and experience fear; 3) unique challenges in paediatric casting, fitting, and gait training required complex decision pathways requiring expert knowledge for component choice and rehabilitation protocols; 4) residual limb challenges and pain, including bone overgrowth, necessitate careful monitoring and proactive socket rectification; 5) lack of appropriately sized and child-specific prosthetic componentry exacerbates rehabilitation challenges due to alignment complications risking undesirable gait patterns; and 6) functional and cosmetic limitations of paediatric componentry restrict optimal participation in childhood activities. This study captures prosthetists' expertise and provides foundational knowledge for junior practitioners and those working in humanitarian settings. It also underscores the need for evidence-based rehabilitation guidelines and improved paediatric prosthetic design.

articles.title: Neuromuscular performance, physiological recovery, and maturation-referenced reference values in youth athletes: A cross-sectional study.
articles.abstract: This cross-sectional study characterized neuromuscular performance and acute physiological responses across age, sex, and biological maturation in 140 youth athletes (74 boys, 66 girls; 10-16 years), and described maturation-stratified distributions of two field measures. Participants completed 30-m sprint, countermovement jump (CMJ), standing long jump (SLJ), and handgrip testing; post-sprint heart-rate recovery (HRrec-30s) and a testing-battery perceived-exertion index (PEI) served as co-primary physiological/perceptual outcomes; maturity offset (Mirwald method) classified Pre-, Circa-, and Post-PHV subgroups; allometric scaling was used to account for body size; and a Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction was applied across a pre-specified family of 58 pairwise comparisons and correlations (Tables 2-6). Boys outperformed girls across all neuromuscular tests (d = 0.63-0.76), whereas HRrec-30s and the perceived-exertion index did not differ significantly by sex. HRrec-30s was more strongly associated with maturity offset than with chronological age (r = 0.52 vs 0.46; η²p for maturation vs age groups 0.43 vs 0.39). Mean HRrec-30s was 27.8 ± 6.2 bpm in the Pre-PHV group and 45.3 ± 8.8 bpm in the Post-PHV group (p < 0.001, FDR-corrected). The perceived-exertion index was lower in more mature groups (7.5 ± 1.2 vs 6.3 ± 1.1). Sex and maturation differences in jump and strength performance remained after allometric scaling, although they were smaller. Maturation-stratified distributions reported here are preliminary and descriptive and are not decision thresholds; prospective, criterion-validated research is needed before they can be recommended for individual athlete monitoring or training-load decision-making.

articles.title: Innovative mHealth intervention providing sustained anticipatory guidance (zero cavity): Design, validation, user perception and effectiveness - A randomized controlled trial protocol.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Early Childhood Caries (ECC) remains one of the most common chronic conditions in childhood, affecting over 600 million children globally. When untreated, it can lead to severe pain, abscesses, difficulty in chewing that contributes to malnutrition, impaired speech, disrupted sleep, low self-esteem, social withdrawal, and poor academic performance, all of which diminish a child's overall quality of life. Although largely preventable, ECC remains highly prevalent because of delayed preventive care and low parental awareness. Effective health education needs to be consistent, accessible, and available whenever parents need it. Although current evidence indicates that anticipatory guidance is a proven approach, its long-term reinforcement through a mobile app has not yet been tested. This study aims to develop and evaluate the effectiveness of a mobile health (mHealth) application delivering Sustained Anticipatory Guidance (SAG) for the prevention of ECC.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: A two-arm parallel hospital-based randomized controlled trial will be conducted at Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education & Research, Chennai, India. The study will enrol 540 mother-infant dyads from the departments of Pediatric Medicine and the Centre for Early Childhood Caries Research (CECCRe). Eligible dyads with infants aged 6-12 months in the predentate stage will be randomized to the "Zero-Cavity" mHealth app (intervention) or standard care (control). Baseline and semi-annual data on oral hygiene, fluoride exposure, and feeding/diet will be collected. Calibrated dentists will perform quarterly clinical exams using ICDAS II criteria, recording cavitated and non-cavitated lesions. For children at high risk or with enamel defects/incipient lesions, clinical photographs will be taken to support individualized preventive guidance. The primary outcome will be the effectiveness of the app in preventing ECC, while the secondary outcomes will include ECC incidence and prevalence.
DISCUSSION: Despite being largely preventable, ECC remains a major public health challenge, sustained by limited preventive access and inconsistent counselling, especially in LMICs. This trial evaluates the Zero Cavity app, believed to bridge this gap by providing sustained, age-appropriate anticipatory guidance beyond clinic settings on oral development, hygiene, diet/feeding, and fluoride use. The behavioural theory-driven approach is expected to enhance cultural relevance, usability, and behaviour change, with optimism that process evaluation will illuminate engagement and implementation. It is believed that this large, adequately powered, parallel-group RCT with intention-to-treat analysis will offer, with optimism, a scalable, low-cost model that will expand the reach and consistency of continuous preventive care in diverse urban and peri-urban populations.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: CTRI/2026/04/107305. Trial access: https://ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?EncHid=MTQyNDEw.

articles.title: Cohort profile: Assessment of factors impacting on foetal and infant immunity, growth, and neurodevelopment in HIV and antiretroviral drug exposed uninfected children: The Siyakhula Study.
articles.abstract: This cohort profile paper describes the Siyakhula cohort, a prospective longitudinal study of mother-child dyads during the ante- and postpartum period. The cohort was established to investigate how in-utero and early postnatal environments altered by maternal HIV status influence infants' growth trajectories, cognitive development, immune development and function, irrespective of the infant's HIV status. Pregnant women aged ≥18 years with singleton pregnancies at <22 weeks' gestation (as per best obstetric estimate, including ultrasound), regardless of HIV status, were recruited from January 2018 to January 2021 and followed throughout pregnancy. After delivery, women were approached for continued enrolment in the postpartum arm, which followed the dyads for 24 months. A total of 315 pregnant women (152 living with HIV and 163 without HIV) were recruited. Routine (pregnancy-related clinical data, HIV status, anthropometry) and research-specific (socio-demographic information, body composition analysis, diet, vaginal swabs, bloods) were collected antepartum. Cord blood and placental samples were collected intrapartum, while breast milk, stool samples, and blood were collected postpartum. Infants had anthropometric measurements performed at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, as well as 6, 12 and 24 months. Neurodevelopmental assessments were conducted during later follow-up visits. Extensive clinical, immunological, metabolomic, nutritional, and developmental data, together with a large biorepository of maternal and infant biospecimens, have been established. This paper provides an overview of the cohort design, participant characteristics, available data and biospecimens, completed analyses, and future research opportunities. Future plans include developing immunometabolic signatures associated with optimal and suboptimal growth and neurodevelopment of infants in the first two years of life.

articles.title: Depressive symptoms among adult patients with systemic lupus erythematosus in the Jazan Region, Saudi Arabia: An analytical cross-sectional study.
articles.abstract: Mental disorders, including depression, are common among patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Depressive symptoms can significantly impair quality of life and are associated with adverse clinical outcomes. Studies investigating depressive symptoms and their associated factors in individuals with SLE have yielded inconsistent findings. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the prevalence of depressive symptoms among patients with SLE and to identify the associated factors in patients from the Jazan Region of Saudi Arabia. An analytical cross-sectional study of 112 patients with SLE in Jazan, Saudi Arabia was conducted in 2023. A convenience sampling technique was used to recruit all eligible adult patients with SLE who attended rheumatology clinics and day-care units at the referral hospitals in the region. Depressive symptoms were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). Chi-square tests and binary logistic regression analyses were used to examine associations and identify factors associated with depressive symptoms. The majority of participants were female (104 [92.9%]), with ages ranging from 18 to 59 years. Depressive symptoms were present in 80% of participants, with patients experiencing mild depression 25 (22%), moderate depression 28 (25%), moderate-to-severe depression 22 (20%), and severe depression 15 (13%).In the multivariable analysis, although physical activity as a categorical variable did not reach overall statistical significance (global p = 0.067), participants engaging in less than 150 minutes of physical activity per week were significantly less likely to experience depressive symptoms compared with those performing no physical activity (OR = 0.28; 95% CI 0.10-0.82; P = 0.020).In conclusion, depressive symptoms were highly prevalent among patients with SLE in the Jazan Region, and physical activity level was identified as a significant modifiable associated factor in this population. Routine screening could facilitate early detection and intervention in patients with SLE in similar settings, resulting in improved clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Dense Granule Protein DG9 of Cryptosporidium parvum Interacts With DG10 at the Dense Band.
articles.abstract: Cryptosporidium parvum, a protozoan parasite, causes life-threatening diarrhea in young children and immunocompromised individuals. During host cell invasion and intracellular proliferation, C. parvum secretes rhoptry, dense granule (DG), and small granule (SG) proteins into the parasite-host interface. These secreted proteins facilitate the biogenesis of the parasitophorous vacuole (PV) enclosing the parasite and the feeder organelle and electron-dense band (DB) at the parasite-host interface. Nevertheless, the molecular compositions of these organelles are poorly defined. Here, we characterized the subcellular localization and functional role of cgd1_470, a highly polymorphic protein associated with host adaptation in the parasite. Using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated endogenous tagging, we revealed that cgd1_470 is a novel DG protein, designated DG9. DG9 is secreted to the parasite-host interface during invasion and localizes to the DB after the PV formation. Deleting the dg9 gene did not significantly alter the in vitro growth or in vivo pathogenicity of a virulent C. parvum strain. Proteomic screening identified several putative DG9-interacting partners, including DG10 (cgd7_4280) and SG5 (cgd1_640), both of which display a similar interfacial localization. We validated the physical interaction between DG9 and DG10 using coimmunoprecipitation and colocalization analyses. Taken together, these findings suggest that DG9 and DG10 are interacting components of the DB at the parasite-host interface.

articles.title: Role of Selected Myokines and Mineral Metabolism in Spinal Muscular Atrophy: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Despite substantial progress in understanding spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), the roles of several biological factors in its pathophysiology remain incompletely characterized. This systematic review aimed to synthesize the current evidence on the role of selected myokines, namely myostatin, follistatin, IL-6 (Interleukin-6), and IGF-1 (Insulin-like growth factor 1), as well as the minerals, copper, zinc, calcium, iron, and magnesium, in the pathogenesis and treatment of SMA. A PROSPERO-registered systematic review included 25 studies. Risk-of-bias assessment using validated tools revealed heterogeneity in methodological quality. The findings suggested that reduced levels of myostatin were associated with disease subtype, functional status, but not with age or 30 months of nusinersen treatment. Follistatin demonstrated protective effects on the neuromuscular system in preclinical models, whereas clinical evidence was inconclusive, with no consistent associations with SMA subtype, age, or body weight. Altered IL-6 levels in blood samples from both children and adults were linked to neuroinflammatory processes and disease activity, suggesting its potential as a biomarker of treatment response. Exogenous IGF-1 attenuated muscle atrophy and improved motor function in preclinical models. Disturbances in mineral homeostasis were related to skeletal and metabolic dysfunction. Studies revealed reduced bone mineral density, magnesium and iron deficiencies, a relationship between copper metabolism and adverse body composition, and the potential neuroprotective role of zinc. Growing evidence suggests that "myokine-mineral crosstalk" may bridge neuromuscular integrity with bone remodeling and calcium-phosphate metabolism in SMA. Overall, these findings provide broader insights into the biological mechanisms underlying SMA pathophysiology and disease monitoring while emphasizing the need for a multidisciplinary research approach.

articles.title: Giving patients a voice: a pilot study of patient-reported outcomes in the Australian cystic fibrosis registry.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To develop, implement, and evaluate a patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) module within the Australian Cystic Fibrosis Data Registry (ACFDR) to enable routine collection of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) data and support clinical care and quality improvement for people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF).
METHODS: This project used a multi-phase mixed methods design to develop, implement, and evaluate a PROMs module within the ACFDR. Study 1 involved co-design with pwCF, caregivers, and clinicians; Study 2 developed and piloted a REDCap-based PROMs module using the tools identified through co-design with pwCF and caregivers; and Study 3 evaluated implementation through a clinician survey.
RESULTS: Participants supported the integration of PROMs into the ACFDR and identified the CFQ-R and AWESCORE as the preferred HRQoL instruments. Priorities for implementation included electronic PROM administration, routine collection of PROM data, and clear reporting of outcomes using these validated measures. During the pilot, 197 (18.7%) of 1,052 invited participants completed the questionnaires. Adults reported generally high HRQoL, except for vitality, health perceptions, and treatment burden. Clinicians supported PROMs collection in the ACFDR, but highlighted challenges including survey fatigue, low response rates, time constraints, and concerns about data quality and representativeness.
CONCLUSION: Integration of PROMs into the ACFDR is feasible and provides valuable insights into the HRQoL of Australians with CF. Future efforts should focus on improving participation and response rates, as well as enhancing data reporting, to maximise the value of PROMs for quality improvement, benchmarking, and patient-centred care.

articles.title: Acute and Early HIV Infection Among Key Populations in Rwanda: A Multisite Cross-Sectional Study to Inform Targeted Testing and Case-Finding, 2025.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute HIV infection is highly transmissible yet often missed by antibody-only rapid tests. Rwanda adopted fourth-generation antigen/antibody (Ag/Ab) tests in 2016, but routine p24 antigen documentation remains limited, limiting acute/early infection estimates. This study characterized acute/early HIV infection among key populations, including female sex workers (FSW), men who have sex with men (MSM), and people who inject drugs (PWID), to inform targeted testing and prevention interventions.
METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study in 2025 across 25 health facilities in 12 Rwandan districts. Individuals aged ≥ 15 years with unknown HIV status from FSW, MSM, PWID, and adolescent girls and young women (AGYW) were recruited via snowball sampling. Structured RedCap questionnaires captured socio-demographic, behavioral, and HIV testing history data. HIV testing followed the national serial algorithm using fourth-generation Determine HIV Early Detect rapid tests; acute/early infection required p24 antigen positivity regardless of antibody status.
RESULTS: Among 1341 participants (median age 25 years, interquartile range [IQR]: 21-30), 864 (64%) were FSW, 177 (13%) were MSM, 58 (4.3%) were PWID, and 242 (18%) were AGYW; 66% had only primary education and 55% resided in rural areas. In the prior 4 weeks, 52% reported multiple sexual partners and 35.5% reported consistent condom use. One-third (416, 32.8%) were aware of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), and 34.7% (141/406) had ever used it. Overall HIV positivity was 5.0% (67/1341); acute/early HIV infection yield was 0.45% (6/1341), with two-thirds of cases (4/6) among MSM, all from Kigali City. Half (3/6) of acute/early cases reported inconsistent condom use and none reported PrEP use.
CONCLUSION: Acute and early HIV infections appear more common among MSM in Kigali, potentially associated with ongoing risk behaviors and low PrEP uptake, although this observation is based on a small number of cases. Priorities include strengthened acute HIV surveillance via fourth-generation and self-testing, rapid antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation, and scaled-up tailored prevention, especially PrEP.

articles.title: Alternative oral therapies join the game against OXA-48 producers: in vitro evidence for cefixime ± amoxicillin/clavulanate in paediatric febrile UTI and mecillinam in lower UTI.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: OXA-48-like carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales are an increasing cause of urinary tract infections (UTIs), limiting oral treatment options. Cefixime activity against OXA-48-like enzymes remains poorly documented, whereas pivmecillinam has shown promising activity in surveillance studies. We assessed the in vitro activity of cefixime, cefixime combined with amoxicillin/clavulanate, mecillinam and mecillinam plus amoxicillin/clavulanate against paediatric OXA-48-like-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, with or without ESBL co-production.
METHODS: We tested 111 non-duplicate paediatric isolates collected in France: 76 E. coli and 35 K. pneumoniae. Isolates were classified as OXA-48-like only, OXA-48-like/ESBL or OXA-48-like with other additional resistance mechanisms. MICs were determined by Etest and mecillinam susceptibility was also assessed by disc diffusion method.
RESULTS: Cefixime was highly active against OXA-48-like-only isolates, with MIC90 values of 0.5 mg/L for E. coli and 0.094 mg/L for K. pneumoniae. Activity decreased markedly in ESBL co-producers (MIC90: 64-256 mg/L), but amoxicillin/clavulanate partially restored activity (MIC90: 2 mg/L for E. coli and 8 mg/L for K. pneumoniae). Mecillinam remained active across groups, with >95% susceptibility among OXA-48-like-only isolates and MIC90 values ≤0.5 mg/L, although susceptibility decreased in isolates with additional resistance mechanisms. Co-resistance to trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and ciprofloxacin was frequent.
CONCLUSIONS: Given frequent co-resistance to standard oral agents and the limited availability of alternatives, cefixime (with or without amoxicillin/clavulanate) and pivmecillinam may represent an oral option for paediatric UTIs caused by OXA-48-like ± ESBL-producing E. coli or K. pneumoniae. Clinical studies will help clarify the potential role of these oral treatment options in paediatric UTIs.

articles.title: Machine Learning Models Using Routine Clinical Data versus Conventional Clinical Scores for Survival Prediction in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Single-Center Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has a poor prognosis, and conventional clinical scores have limited accuracy in predicting individualized survival.
PURPOSE: We aimed to determine whether machine learning (ML) models using routine clinical data discriminate survival better than established clinical scores in HCC and to compare the prognostic profiles of MASLD- and HBV-associated HCC.
METHODS: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of 233 patients with HCC diagnosed between 2010 and 2026. Patients with valid survival data and ≤20% missingness across 29 pre-specified predictor variables were included. During a median follow-up of 15 months, 143 patients died. Random Survival Forest, XGBoost, a Hybrid ensemble model, and penalized Cox regression were trained using 5-fold cross-validation. Model discrimination was assessed using Harrell's C-index and the fixed-horizon AUROC. The score-excluded V2 analysis removed clinical scores from ML inputs. SHAP values quantified feature contributions.
RESULTS: The best-performing ML model (Hybrid) achieved a C-index of 0.797, higher than BCLC stage (0.735), Child-Pugh class, and ALBI grade, but only modestly higher than penalized Cox regression with the same variables (0.773). In the score-excluded sensitivity analysis, the Random Survival Forest maintained a strong performance (C-index 0.784). The best fixed-horizon 12-month AUROC was 0.878. SHAP analysis identified AFP, ECOG performance status, albumin, tumor diameter, and total bilirubin as the most influential predictors. Among 57 patients with MASLD-associated HCC, the median survival was 23.0 months vs 54.0 months in 116 patients with HBV-associated HCC (p=0.0328); this difference was not explained by age, comorbidities, tumor characteristics, or treatment.
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-center cohort, models using routinely available variables discriminated survival in HCC better than conventional clinical scores by combining more information.

articles.title: Perspectives of parents of children with monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders on research involving patient-derived neuronal models.
articles.abstract: Patient-derived stem cell-based neuronal models hold great promise for advancing research into monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders (mNDDs). These neuronal models are generated using induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) technologies, and are perceived as "ethically sensitive". To date, ethical discussions on the use of neuronal models have predominantly focused on three-dimensional (3D) neuronal models, such as brain organoids, while two-dimensional (2D) neuronal models - which are widely used in current research settings - remain underexplored. A better understanding of the perspectives of parents of children with mNDDs on ethical issues - including the moral status of 2D models, informed consent, autonomy, privacy and misuse - is needed. We report the results of a semi-structured interview study among parents of children with mNDDs (n = 28) investigating their perspectives on the ethically responsible use of 2D patient-derived neuronal models in research. Respondents ascribed limited intrinsic value to neuronal models, often viewing them as ethically comparable to other somatic cells. They were highly motivated to enroll their child in iPSC research, but suggested that researchers: (1) restrict the use of their child's donated material to purposes benefiting the mNDD community, (2) protect their child's privacy, (3) communicate about research findings and reuse of donated material, and (4) minimize risks and burdens of research procedures for their (vulnerable) child. Based on these findings, we provide recommendations to research groups for informed consent and engagement processes to support responsible inclusion of children with mNDDs and their families in research using iPSC-based neuronal models.

articles.title: Clinical recommendations on monitoring and management of bone health in adults with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy and transition to adult care: A national Delphi consensus study.
articles.abstract: Poor bone health and low-trauma fractures are common in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), reflecting the combined effects of progressive muscle weakness, reduced mechanical loading, delayed puberty and/or hypogonadism, and long-term glucocorticoid exposure. Although paediatric bone health guidance in DMD is well established, adult-specific recommendations remain limited, particularly for individuals who enter adult services having received many years of bisphosphonate therapy during childhood or adolescence. We developed national expert consensus recommendations for the monitoring and management of bone health in adults with DMD, with particular emphasis on transition from paediatric to adult care. Recommendations were informed by review of the literature, a clinician survey, input from adults with DMD and carers, and discussion within a multidisciplinary expert group. A modified Delphi process was undertaken, with 16 clinicians voting on draft statements using a 9-point agreement scale; consensus was defined as at least 80% of participants scoring 7-9. Thirteen evidence-informed expert consensus clinical recommendations were agreed, covering fracture risk assessment, DXA and vertebral fracture monitoring, vitamin D and gonadal status, indications for specialist bone review, initiation and review of osteoporosis therapy, management of possible treatment failure, and structured review of long-term therapy during transition. The recommendations emphasise individualised decision-making, recognising the technical challenges of imaging, limited adult DMD-specific evidence, cumulative treatment burden, and the functional impact of fractures in this population. These consensus recommendations provide a practical framework to support adult neuromuscular and bone clinicians managing bone health in a rare, high-risk and increasingly adult DMD population.

articles.title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics reveal glycolytic remodeling and ENO1-associated metabolic vulnerability in hepatoblastoma.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hepatoblastoma (HB) is the most common malignant liver tumor in children; however, the contribution of glycolytic metabolic reprogramming to HB development and progression remains incompletely characterized.
METHODS: We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic datasets of HB from the GEO database. Glycometabolic pathway activity was quantified using scMetabolism, and pseudotime and transcription factor activity analyses were performed to characterize regulatory programs associated with glycolytic reprogramming. CellChat and spatial transcriptomics were applied to examine predicted tumor-immune communication. hdWGCNA combined with differential expression analysis was used to prioritize glycolysis-associated genes. ENO1 was further evaluated by in silico network perturbation, two independent shRNAs in vitro, and computational compound prioritization followed by molecular docking and a 100-ns molecular dynamics simulation.
RESULTS: The single-cell atlas resolved 10 major cell types and revealed elevated glycolysis/gluconeogenesis pathway scores in malignant epithelial cells. Pseudotime analysis showed increasing glycolytic activity along the inferred epithelial trajectory. CellChat predicted enhanced MDK-NCL communication between Glyco_High tumor cells and neutrophils, while spatial analysis showed regional concordance between MDK/NCL co-expression and high-glycolysis areas. hdWGCNA identified three glycolysis-associated candidate genes: ENO1, AKR1A1, and AHCY. In silico ENO1 perturbation was associated with altered inferred regulatory activity of approximately 2.1% of genes. Two independent ENO1-targeting shRNAs produced concordant reductions in proliferation, colony formation, lactate production, and glucose consumption in HepG2 and Huh6 cells. BRD-K14653796 was computationally prioritized, and the modeled ENO1-compound complex remained conformationally stable under the specified simulation conditions.
CONCLUSIONS: This study characterizes glycolytic heterogeneity in HB at single-cell and spatial resolution and nominates ENO1 as a candidate metabolic vulnerability in CNV-high putative malignant epithelial cells. It also highlights a computationally predicted MDK-NCL-associated tumor-immune communication pattern and provides testable hypotheses for future preclinical validation.

articles.title: A multicenter study of capsule endoscopy in preschool children in China.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the safety and clinical utility of capsule endoscopy in preschool-aged children.
METHODS: A multicenter retrospective study design was used, including data from eight specialized pediatric hospitals in China. Children aged < 6 years who were hospitalized and underwent capsule endoscopy between January 2020 and August 2025 were included.
RESULTS: This study included 155 patients (mean age 56.9 ± 14.2 months). The most common indication was chronic abdominal pain (50.97%), followed by suspected inflammatory bowel disease (22.58%), gastrointestinal bleeding (16.13%), and unexplained anemia (8.39%). Abnormal findings were identified in 69 cases, which established a definitive diagnosis in 55 patients (diagnostic yield, 35.5%), including 15 with isolated small-bowel disease. Capsule retention occurred in three patients with Crohn's disease. Fifty patients swallowed the capsule independently, while others required endoscopic placement; endoscopic assistance increased the success rate of capsule delivery to 100% in preschool children. When preschool children exhibited elevated inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein(CRP) 6 mg/L [interquartile range (IQR), 0.81-23 mg/L] vs. 0.95 mg/L [IQR, 0.51-3.58 mg/L]; erythrocyte sedimentation rate(ESR) 16 mm/h [IQR, 6-27 mm/h] vs. 7 mm/h [IQR, 4-14 mm/h]), lower albumin levels (38.47 ± 8.83 g/L vs. 42.50 ± 4.92 g/L), and intestinal wall thickening on imaging (56.36% vs. 20.00%), the diagnostic positive rate significantly increased.
CONCLUSIONS: Capsule endoscopy is safe for preschool children. Capsule retention is mainly associated with underlying diseases. Capsule endoscopy is recommended to assess small-bowel lesions in children with elevated inflammatory markers, reduced albumin levels, or radiographic evidence of bowel wall thickening, facilitating early diagnosis and treatment.

articles.title: Role of small intestinal bacteria overgrowth in irritable bowel syndrome and anxiety: a retrospective Electronic Health Record (EHR)- based cohort study using triNetX.
articles.abstract:
AIMS: The goal of this study is to examine the relationship between small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) with their subsequent risk of developing generalized anxiety disorder (GAD).
METHODOLOGY: Data for this retrospective study was obtained through TriNetX, a global health research network that aggregates de-identified electronic health records from over 100 million patients across multiple healthcare organizations. Two cohorts of 7716 patients were identified. Cohort 1 consisted of IBS patients with SIBO and Cohort 2 consisted of IBS patients without SIBO. Patients included were aged 18 to 50 years. Patients with pre-existing diagnoses of GAD, panic disorder, or depressive episodes before IBS onset were excluded. Cohorts were matched for sex, race, ethnicity, gastroesophageal reflux disease, non-infective enteritis and colitis, and proton pump inhibitor use through logistic regression models.
RESULTS: IBS patients with SIBO (Cohort 1) demonstrated a GAD incidence of 6.36% compared to 4.71% in those without SIBO (Cohort 2), yielding an absolute risk difference of 1.66% (95% CI: 0.938%-2.38%, p<0.0001). Logistic regression revealed an odds ratio of 1.377 (95% CI: 1.197-1.583) for GAD development in Cohort 1. Cox proportional hazards modeling demonstrated a hazard ratio of 1.301 (95% CI: 1.136-1.491, p=0.0008), indicating that IBS patients with SIBO faced a significantly elevated and persistent risk of GAD development over the 15-year observation period.
DISCUSSION: IBS patients with comorbid SIBO have a significantly elevated risk of developing GAD compared to IBS patients without SIBO. These findings suggest that SIBO may amplify gut-brain axis dysfunction beyond what is observed in IBS alone.

articles.title: Electrocardiographic abnormalities associated with obesity in adolescents and young adults: physiologic variants or true pathology? A cross-sectional study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Obesity is defined by the World Health Organization as abnormal or excessive fat accumulation that poses a risk to health. It has reached epidemic proportions globally and carries significant cardiovascular risk, particularly in adolescents and young adults. Electrocardiographic (ECG) changes are well documented in obese adults; however, the extent and nature of these changes in healthy obese and non-obese young people remain poorly characterized. This study aimed to determine whether obesity-related ECG abnormalities are confined to obese adolescents and young adults or are equally observed across other body mass index (BMI) categories.
METHODS: A cross-sectional descriptive study was conducted among 172 apparently healthy participants aged 10 to 24 years, recruited using a multi-stage stratified random sampling method. Participants were categorized into three BMI groups (normal weight, overweight and obese) according to CDC-BMI percentile for age criteria. A 12-lead resting ECG was performed on each participant using a Grandfield Medical three-channel ECG machine with automated analysis secondarily validated by a clinician. Anthropometric, clinical, and biochemical parameters were also obtained. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 23.0, and a p-value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
RESULTS: Females constituted 59.3% of participants (M: F ratio approximately 1:1.5), with a mean age of 18.1 years (SD 3.77) and mean BMI of 27.2 kg/m² (SD 5.74). ECG abnormalities were observed overall in 43% of participants after excluding physiologic variants. Statistically significant findings included prolonged P-wave duration consistent with left atrial enlargement (p = 0.01), prolonged PR interval (p = 0.025), and T-wave flattening in inferior and lateral leads (p = 0.017). T-wave flattening was most prevalent in the normal BMI group (42%). Age-related differences were identified for pulse rate and early repolarization pattern (ERP), both were significantly higher in early adolescents aged 10 to 14 years (p < 0.001). P-axis values were significantly higher in young adults aged 20 to 24 years than in middle adolescents aged 15 to 19 years (p = 0.005). T-axis measurements was significantly greater in males than females (p = 0.016). Other findings including arrhythmias, left ventricular hypertrophy, right ventricular hypertrophy, atrial enlargement, and early repolarization pattern (ERP) were observed but did not reach statistical significance across BMI groups. QTc interval and QRS voltage were normal across all groups.
CONCLUSION: The majority of ECG findings observed in this study are consistent with physiologic variants distributed across all BMI categories. These findings are not confined to obese individuals, which challenges the assumption that such ECG changes are obesity-specific. Early screening in this age group may assist in differentiating true cardiac pathology from normal physiological variants, which has normal healthy spectrum of body functions or structure and requires no treatment modality because it represent the natural range of human diversity.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

articles.title: Early Motor Pattern Analysis Using a Single RGB-D Camera: A Case Study of Twins at Divergent Risk for Motor Impairment.
articles.journal: IEEE Open J Eng Med Biol
articles.abstract: Early identification of motor impairment in infants at developmental risk can benefit from objective assessment methods. In this feasibility study, we evaluated quantitative kinematic metrics extracted from home-based recordings as indicators of developmental differences between twins with divergent perinatal outcomes. Two 4-month-old twins, one typically developing and one at-risk of motor impairment, were recorded using a single RGB-D camera at home. Videos of up to three minutes per twin were captured at seven timepoints, about 30 days apart. Seven upper body points of interest were tracked using DeepLabCut and their 3D coordinates calculated with an improved version of a previously published method adapted for home use. Thirteen metrics were estimated at each timepoint. Most metrics were consistent with the trends reported in the literature, distinguishing divergent perinatal outcomes. These findings demonstrated that the proposed method is usable for home-based data collection, compensating for motion artifacts and reducing manual labeling time.

articles.title: The association between binge eating and the metabolic profile of adolescents with obesity.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIM: Binge eating (BE) might further deteriorate the inflammatory and metabolic profile of individuals with obesity, but data in adolescents are limited and inconsistent. This study aimed to compare the metabolic and inflammatory parameters of adolescents with and without BE and to investigate the relationship between BE and metabolic syndrome.
METHODS AND RESULTS: A total of 82 adolescents (12-18 years) with overweight or obesity were evaluated for the presence of BE through the Munich Eating and Nutritional Disorders Questionnaire. Waist circumference, BMI z-score, systolic and diastolic blood pressure measurements, a range of biomarkers including fasting and postprandial glucose and insulin, lipid profile, liver enzymes, thyroid function, and inflammatory markers were measured. BE episodes were reported by 47.6% of participants and were more prevalent in females (p = 0.041). Elevated blood pressure was more common in the BE group (p = 0.021). No significant differences were found in anthropometric measures, laboratory findings, or overall metabolic syndrome prevalence between the BE and non-BE groups. In univariable logistic regression analysis, BE was associated with elevated blood pressure (OR = 4.59, 95% CI: 1.61-18.20, p = 0.030). In the multivariable model, only waist circumference remained significant (OR = 1.14, 95% CI: 1.04-1.25, p = 0.004).
CONCLUSIONS: While univariable analysis suggested a potential relationship between BE and elevated blood pressure, this association was attenuated after accounting for adiposity-related factors. Larger longitudinal follow-up studies are needed to clarify the temporal relationship between BE and cardiometabolic risk factors and assess whether BE predicts future development of metabolic syndrome.

articles.title: Human herpesvirus 7-associated encephalitis diagnosed by metagenomic next-generation sequencing in pediatric patients: a retrospective study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The objective of this study was to describe the clinical features, treatment and prognosis of immunocompetent children with human herpes virus 7 (HHV-7)-associated encephalitis.
METHODS: Sixteen children with HHV-7-associated encephalitis were diagnosed by metagenomic next-generation sequencing of their cerebrospinal fluid and followed up for 3 months.
RESULTS: The median age of the cohort was 8.6 years (range, 1.4-11.8) and comprised of 8 males and 8 females. The most common presenting symptoms were fever (12/16, 75.0%), headache (10/16, 62.5%), and vomiting (8/16, 50.0%). Abnormal electroencephalography and encephalitis-related neuroimaging findings were obtained in 50.0% (6/12) and 25.0% (4/16) of the patients, respectively. 68.8% of the patients were treated with either acyclovir or ganciclovir. Unfavorable outcomes occurred in three patients, including the death of a 2-year-old child.
CONCLUSION: Pediatric HHV-7-associated encephalitis generally has a favorable prognosis, but severe cases do occur. Early recognition is important for increasing clinicians' awareness of this condition.

articles.title: The role of personal exposure to stroke in stroke awareness among Palestinian university students: a cross-sectional study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early recognition of stroke symptoms is critical to ensuring a timely emergency response and access to acute stroke therapies that must be administered within specific time windows. Personal exposure to stroke may enhance stroke awareness by increasing perceived susceptibility and severity, and fostering experiential learning. This study investigated whether a family history of stroke and personal acquaintance with a stroke survivor were associated with stroke knowledge among Palestinian university students.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study included undergraduate students from four universities in West Bank in May 2026. Knowledge was measured using an Arabic translation of the 20-item Stroke Knowledge Test (SKT) that had not been formally validated. Participants were grouped into three categories: no exposure, knowing someone with exposure only, or having both family history and personal knowledge of a survivor. Multiple linear regression was used to analyze the continuous score (0-20), adjusting for sex, age, university, and academic field. Logistic regression was also used to examine a study-defined, unvalidated threshold of ≥10/20.
RESULTS: Of the 393 students, 86.3% were enrolled in health sciences. A total of 205 (52.2%) reported neither a family history of stroke nor knowing a stroke survivor, 129 (32.8%) knew a stroke survivor but had no family history of stroke, and 59 (15.0%) reported both a family history of stroke and knowing a stroke survivor. Mean scores were 11.59 ± 4.88, 12.48 ± 4.47, and 13.17 ± 3.77, respectively (p = 0.038). Compared with no exposure, adjusted scores were higher among those who knew someone only (B = 0.98, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.09-1.88; p = 0.031) and among those with both exposures (B = 1.26, 95% CI: 0.08-2.45; p = 0.036). The corresponding odds ratios (ORs) for meeting the study-defined threshold were 2.33 (95% CI: 1.29-4.22) and 2.90 (95% CI: 1.23-6.84).
CONCLUSION: Personal exposure to stroke was associated with higher knowledge scores in this sample, which consisted predominantly of health sciences students. The continuous score analysis supports an association independent of the study-defined cutoff. The unvalidated Arabic adaptation and the use of convenience sampling limit interpretation and generalizability. Survivor-based educational approaches warrant evaluation.

articles.title: Functional stabilization with ataluren in ambulatory children with nonsense mutation Duchenne muscular dystrophy: a real-world ambispective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
