High CSNS remained an independent predictor of mortality (adjusted HR 1.023; p = 0.002) and was significantly associated with major cirrhosis-related complications, including hepatic encephalopathy, acute kidney injury, refractory ascites, and upper gastrointestinal bleeding (all p ≤ 0.003).
CONCLUSION: The CSNS is a simple, radiation-free bedside tool that improves prognostic assessment beyond conventional scores and may support risk stratification in resource-limited settings.

articles.title: Turkish Adaptation and Psychometric Evaluation of the Oral Health-Related Quality of Life Measure for Children/Adolescents With Down Syndrome (OH-QOLADS).
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to adapt the Oral Health-Related Quality of Life for Adolescents with Down Syndrome (OH-QOLADS) scale into Turkish and evaluate its psychometric properties. It also explored oral health status and quality of life among children with Down syndrome (DS).
METHODS: The study included 100 children with DS and their mothers. Sociodemographic and oral health data were collected through structured questionnaires. The OH-QOLADS, comprising child and family forms with two timeframes, was translated and culturally adapted following international guidelines. Internal consistency, CFA, and item-total correlations were conducted to assess psychometric validity.
RESULTS: The Turkish OH-QOLADS showed excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's α and McDonald's ω > 0.94) across all forms and timeframes. CFA supported the original four-factor structure (symptoms/functioning, emotional well-being, social participation, and family impact) with strong model fit indices (CFI > 0.98; RMSEA < 0.05). Most participants reported poor oral health, low tooth brushing frequency, and minimal preventive care. Oral health-related quality of life (OHRQoL) scores were significantly associated with comorbidities like thyroid disease, diabetes, and hearing impairments.
CONCLUSION: The Turkish OH-QOLADS is a valid, reliable tool for assessing OHRQoL in children with DS. The findings highlight the need for better access to preventive dental services and caregiver support.

articles.title: From Skin Commensals to Bloodstream Pathogens: In Vitro Virulence Traits and In Vivo Pathogenicity of Malassezia Isolates.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The lipid-dependent yeast genus Malassezia is composed of skin commensals that can become pathogenic. This genus can cause bloodstream infection in low-weight preterm neonates and immunocompromised adults. However, little is known about the virulence mechanism involved in the transition from commensal to pathogenic.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate and compare the in vitro and in vivo virulence of M. furfur, M. pachydermatis and M. sympodialis strains from fungemia cases and healthy skin or superficial clinical entities.
METHODS: Twenty-five isolates, along with three reference strains of the three evaluated species, were assessed in vitro for virulence traits, including phospholipase and hemolytic activity, thermotolerance, oxidative stress resistance and biofilm production. Those isolates that presented the highest or lowest in vitro virulence based on the evaluated traits were evaluated in vivo in the Galleria mellonella infection model.
RESULTS: Fungemia isolates of the three species showed higher phospholipase activity, biofilm formation, thermotolerance and oxidative stress resistance. Only for M. furfur, a high hemolytic activity was registered for the fungemia isolate. In vivo evaluation supported the previous in vitro results, in which larvae inoculated with isolates from fungemia and with high in vitro virulence were demonstrated to induce higher mortality and tissue burden, contrasting with isolates from healthy skin or skin clinical entities.
CONCLUSION: The evaluated isolates exhibited heterogeneous in vitro phenotypes and experimental pathogenicity. The findings support further investigation of relationships between these traits and infection outcomes. Finally, M. furfur showed a higher capacity to survive in the host, correlating with the Malassezia-fungemia epidemiology.

articles.title: Child Sexual Abuse, Sexual Function, and Sexual Distress in Couples Coping with Sexual Interest/Arousal Disorder: A Dyadic Longitudinal Study.
articles.abstract: Sexual interest/arousal disorder (SIAD), characterized by low sexual desire and high sexual distress, is the most common sexual dysfunction among women. Although current theoretical models support interpersonal conceptualizations of sexual desire, distal interpersonal factors that may underlie the sexual well-being of couples coping with SIAD, such as child sexual abuse (CSA), have not been thoroughly documented. Yet, difficulties with sexual desire and arousal are among the most frequently reported sexual dysfunctions among CSA survivors. Using a one-year longitudinal design among couples with SIAD, this study examined the associations between both partners' CSA and their sexual function and distress. Individuals with SIAD (N = 263; Mage = 34.16) and their partners (N = 263; Mage = 35.71) completed validated questionnaires at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months. Dyadic latent growth curve analyses were conducted within a structural equation model. Results showed that greater CSA among individuals with SIAD was associated with their own higher initial levels of sexual distress. Moreover, higher levels of non-SIAD partners' CSA were unexpectedly associated with lower initial levels of sexual function difficulties for individuals with SIAD. However, non-SIAD partners' CSA predicted greater increases in sexual function difficulties over time for individuals with SIAD. No other significant associations were found. Findings highlight the role of CSA in the sexual function and distress of couples coping with SIAD and point towards the value of couple-based interventions that acknowledge both partners' histories and their impact on mutual sexual experiences.

articles.title: Chest Pain in Children and Adolescents in the Emergency Department: A State-of-the-Art Narrative Review of Epidemiology, Risk Stratification, and Evidence-Based Management.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chest pain accounts for approximately 0.5%-1% of pediatric emergency department (ED) visits and is a frequent source of anxiety for families and clinicians. Although concern for cardiac disease often drives evaluation, true cardiac etiologies are rare, typically representing only 1%-2.5% of cases. The challenge in pediatric emergency care lies in distinguishing the small subset of patients with potentially life-threatening conditions from the large majority with benign causes, while avoiding unnecessary testing and radiation exposure.
METHODS: We conducted a state-of-the-art narrative review synthesizing contemporary literature on the epidemiology, differential diagnosis, cardiac risk stratification, diagnostic testing, and emerging technologies relevant to pediatric chest pain evaluation in the ED. Emphasis was placed on structured clinical assessment and evidence-based use of diagnostic modalities.
RESULTS: Most pediatric chest pain is noncardiac, with musculoskeletal causes predominating, followed by psychogenic, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal etiologies. Cardiac causes remain uncommon but require systematic identification through careful history, focused physical examination, and electrocardiography. High-risk features include exertional pain, syncope, abnormal examination findings, concerning family history, and abnormal ECG results. Standardized clinical pathways reduce unnecessary imaging and cardiac testing without compromising diagnostic safety. Chest radiography and troponin testing have limited utility when used indiscriminately, whereas point-of-care ultrasound offers a radiation-free adjunct in selected cases. Emerging tools such as teletriage and artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostics show promise but require further validation in pediatric populations.
CONCLUSION: Pediatric chest pain is usually benign but necessitates structured, risk-stratified evaluation to safely exclude serious disease. Judicious testing guided by clinical assessment improves efficiency, minimizes radiation exposure, and supports high-value, patient-centered emergency care.

articles.title: Does Child Marriage Mediate the Relationship Between Experiencing Pre-Marital Sexual Intercourse and the Discontinuation of Education or Employment?
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: In low- and middle-income countries, girls are more likely than boys to drop out of school when they become sexually mature and particularly when they engage in or experience premarital sexual intercourse. This study aims to examine whether child marriage mediates the relationship between premarital sexual intercourse and the discontinuation of education or employment among women.
METHOD: Data on ever-married women aged 15-49 years were extracted from the Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey 2022. Data were available for 13,778 ever-married women, enabling an assessment of whether they experienced premarital sexual intercourse and whether they continued their education or employment after marriage. The mediating effect of child marriage was examined by using the "mediate" command available in Stata software.
RESULTS: Overall, child marriage was significantly more prevalent among those who had sexual intercourse before marriage than among those who reported it after marriage (81% vs 59%). Approximately 81% of women who were engaged or experienced premarital sexual intercourse were married before the age of 18, and 17.02% reported that they continued their education or employment after marriage. Among the women who experienced sexual intercourse during or after marriage (n = 9,640), nearly 59% got married before the age of 18, and 16.72% of these women continued their education or employment after getting married.
CONCLUSIONS: Child marriage is a significant mediator in the relationship between premarital sexual intercourse and the cessation of education or employment. Premarital sexual intercourse substantially influences child marriage, which then affects cessation of education and employment. Since educational achievements for girls have broader positive effects, raising awareness of the impacts of child marriage, enhancing sexual health literacy, and improving access to contraception for adolescents are urgently needed.

articles.title: Experiences of Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health in Two Rural Kenyan Communities.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Global adolescent sexual and reproductive health (SRH) disparities persist despite international attention and guidelines to address them. Significant investments to address adolescent health have been made in Kenya using innovative approaches at the intersection of policy, community, and the healthcare sector. Despite these significant investments, Kenya continues to experience high rates of adolescent pregnancy. The aim of this study was to describe barriers to adolescent sexual health and elicit suggestions to improve adolescent SRH outcomes in rural Kenya.
METHODS: This qualitative study purposively recruited participants to represent key stakeholder groups including adolescents, parents, teachers, faith leaders, and healthcare workers to participate in focus group discussions. Each focus group followed a semi-structured interview guide focused on barriers to adolescent sexual and reproductive health and suggestions for improvement. Following data collection, digital recordings were translated as needed and transcribed into English. The research team collaboratively coded the data using thematic analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 15 focus groups were conducted ranging in size from 5 to 12 participants and lasted 30 minutes to 2 hours. Findings were grouped into two main themes to describe barriers to adolescent SRH and recommendations to improve adolescent SRH. Barriers included cultural norms, gender, lack of understanding of adolescent development and limited access to sexual and reproductive health information and services. Suggestions for improvement included alternative rites of passage ceremonies for transition to adulthood, gender-specific SRH education and programming, training and support for adults to foster healthy adolescent sexual development, and encouragement and support for adolescent mothers return to school.
CONCLUSION: The findings from this study underscore the multifaceted and deeply rooted challenges influencing adolescent SRH in Kenya. Only through coordinated action and inclusive dialogue can the country create an enabling environment where adolescents are informed, empowered, and protected in their journey toward adulthood.

articles.title: Gender-Specific Patterns of Sexual Health Outcomes and Associated Factors: A Cross-Sectional School-Based Study with Adolescents in Brazil.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To analyze the socioeconomic, individual, school behavior, family behavior, and health risk factors associated with sexual health outcomes among Brazilian adolescents.
METHODS: This was a cross-sectional, school-based study with a representative sample of 4514 adolescents aged 14-19. Data were collected using the Global School-based Student Health Survey (GSHS). The outcomes were early sexual debut (≤14 years), multiple sexual partners (≥2), and condom nonuse at last intercourse. A composite binary variable for accumulated sexual health indicators was also created. Multilevel binary logistic regression was used to identify associated factors, stratified by sex.
RESULTS: Boys had significantly higher prevalences of early sexual debut (19.4%) and multiple partners (32.1%). For both sexes, alcohol and drug use, as well as living with one or neither parent, were strongly associated with all sexual health outcomes. However, gender-specific factors were identified. For girls, low maternal education and urban residence were associated with sexual health outcomes. For boys, school absenteeism and leisure-time physical activity were consistently associated with sexual health outcomes. The magnitude of association with substance use was consistently higher for boys.
CONCLUSIONS: Sexual health outcomes among Brazilian adolescents are shaped by a complex interplay of factors with distinct gender-specific patterns. These findings underscore the need for integrated, gender-sensitive health promotion strategies in schools that address substance use and family context to effectively reduce vulnerabilities.

articles.title: Social Media, Skin Appearance, and Adolescent Psychosexual Health: A Dermatologic Perspective.
articles.abstract: Adolescence is a period of intensive biologic and psychosocial development during which physical appearance becomes especially important for self-esteem, peer relationships, and identity formation. Social media increases the exposure of adolescents to idealized representations of appearance, including skin without acne, erythema, pigmentation, or scarring. This may be especially relevant for young people with visible dermatoses whose actual appearance differs from the digitally modified representations. This contribution discusses associations between social media use, body image, skin appearance, and adolescent psychosexual health, especially to acne, atopic dermatitis, and psoriasis. It considers the potential roles of social comparison, internalization of attractiveness standards, sexualization of appearance, and stress related to the evaluation of one's skin. Clinical implications are also addressed, including attempts to conceal lesions, unrealistic expectations of dermatological treatment and skin care, and the possibility of substantial appearance-related distress. Available evidence does not justify attributing these outcomes exclusively to social media; however, it supports taking the digital environment into account when assessing adolescents with visible skin diseases.

articles.title: Beauty Algorithms and AI Filters in Adolescent Body Image Disturbance: Dermatologic and Psychologic Consequences.
articles.abstract: Adolescence is a period of increased vulnerability to changes in body image, while visible skin features, including acne, pigmentation, and scarring, may have substantial social and psychologic significance. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based beauty filters enable simultaneous modification of skin texture and complexion and facial proportions, creating a digital representation that may differ substantially from actual appearance. This study examines the potential dermatologic and psychologic consequences of AI beauty filters in adolescents, with particular attention to discrepancies between actual and digitally modified appearance. The roles of social comparison, internalization of appearance ideals, self-objectification, and self-discrepancy in shaping body image are discussed. Current evidence suggests associations between appearance-focused social media activity, photo editing, and appearance dissatisfaction; however, evidence specifically concerning AI beauty filters remains limited and heterogeneous, with a substantial proportion of available studies involving adults. From a dermatologic perspective, AI filters may influence perceptions of acne, pigmentation, scarring, and skin texture and may shape expectations involving dermatologic treatment and aesthetic procedures. Additional longitudinal research of the adolescent population is needed to examine the relationships between repeated exposure to filtered representations of appearance, psychologic factors, and objectivel assessed skin status.

articles.title: Family Factors in Sibling Sexual Abuse: A Comparative Study With Interfamilial and Peer Child Sexual Abuse.
articles.abstract: Sibling sexual abuse (SSA) cases were compared with two other types of child sexual abuse (CSA): sexual abuse by an adult family member and sexual abuse by a peer to identify differences in individual, family, abuse, and actor characteristics. In addition, differences in parental responses upon disclosure were examined given the importance of parental support for long-term trauma processing of children. Data from 131 client records from a children's mental health center were used, with 43 to 44 records per type of CSA. Results suggested some specific individual and family characteristics associated with SSA, including a larger family size, delayed disclosure, parental reluctance to place accountability with the sibling who has harmed, more ongoing contact between the harmed child and the sibling who has harmed, and the co-occurrence of child maltreatment. A limitation is that clinical records reflect a self-selective sample of families who voluntarily reached out for professional help, limiting the generalizability of findings to sibling sexual abuse cases that typically remain undisclosed. However, this may simultaneously enhance the relevance of our findings for professionals supporting families that have experienced SSA. The findings underscore the need for systemic interventions that take into account the emotional bonds between siblings, parent-child relationships, and the complex family dynamics that are associated with the abuse.

articles.title: Echoes of Trauma: The Role of Self-Esteem Between Adverse Childhood Experiences and Intimate Partner Violence Victimization.
articles.abstract: The association between adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and intimate partner violence victimization (IPVV) is well-documented. However, little is known about whether this association varies by self-esteem during emerging adulthood, a developmental period marked by increasing self-exploration and exposure to intimate relationships. This study examines whether self-esteem moderates the association between ACEs and IPVV in emerging adulthood. Data were drawn from South Korean emerging adults aged 18 to 29 with dating experience (N = 953). Negative binomial regression models were estimated, followed by average marginal effects and Johnson-Neyman style floodlight analysis. The results show that the association between physical ACEs and physical IPVV was significantly positive at lower levels of self-esteem. However, two disjoint crossover patterns were found between neglect and emotional IPVV (EIPVV). Neglect was negatively associated with EIPVV at a lower level of self-esteem but positively associated at a higher level. Findings highlight subtype-specific ACE-IPVV pathways and caution against treating self-esteem as a uniformly protective factor. The study contributes to trauma-informed IPVV prevention by emphasizing the need to consider both childhood adversity histories and the quality of self-esteem during emerging adulthood.

articles.title: Adult-pretrained activity recognition across paediatric datasets: target adaptation and wheelchair activity coverage.
articles.abstract: Adult-pretrained models may support paediatric activity recognition, but their performance across datasets and activities remains uncertain. We evaluated harnet10 using thigh accelerometry from 46 typically developing children and 31 children and adolescents with mobility impairments. Training and testing involved separate participants. Source fine tuning achieved participant-equal macro-F1 of 0.904, compared with 0.842 for random initialisation. In the target dataset, five-seed logit ensembles achieved F1 of 0.373 for direct transfer and 0.678 for fine tuning. Fine tuning used five labelled windows per class selected from a fully annotated pool. Across 20 repetitions with independently sampled support sets in each fold, mean F1 was 0.594, compared with 0.372 for matched direct transfer. Each repetition averaged participant-normalised confusion matrices across three optimisation seeds, so the two analyses differed in both support sets and prediction aggregation. Adaptation improved F1 in every repetition and after excluding wheelchair-leading mixed windows. Among 18 participants with wheelchair activity, uncertainty ranking achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.801. The seven-class model predicted no wheelchair windows, giving zero wheelchair recall and F1. Adult pretraining and limited target supervision improved recognition of shared activities in these cohorts. The wheelchair findings highlight the need for activity-specific validation before clinical use.

articles.title: Redefining glucose thresholds for hypoglycaemia management in children and young adults with type 1 diabetes on automated insulin therapy: A cross-over clinical trial protocol.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIM: Current international guidelines for hypoglycaemia management in Type 1 diabetes recommend initiating treatment when glucose level falls below 3.9 mmol/L. However, these recommendations were developed before widespread use of diabetes technologies. This study aims to determine whether a revised hypoglycaemia treatment approach incorporating a lower treatment threshold is non-inferior to the standard threshold (<3.9 mmol/L) in children and young adults with Type 1 diabetes using automated insulin delivery (AID) systems. We hypothesise that the revised approach will be non-inferior to the current standard recommendations without increasing time in clinically significant hypoglycaemia.
METHODS: This single-centre, randomised, two-period, crossover, non-inferiority trial will recruit 45 participants aged 6-25 years with Type 1 diabetes, diagnosed for at least 12 months and using AID systems. Participants will complete two 4-week treatment periods in random order: standard hypoglycaemia treatment (<3.9 mmol/L) and revised hypoglycaemia treatment (≤3.6 mmol/L with consideration of CGM trends, active insulin, exercise and symptoms). Treatment periods will be separated by a 2-week washout period. The primary outcome is the percentage of time spent in clinically significant hypoglycaemia (<3.0 mmol/L), measured using CGM. Secondary outcomes are CGM metrics including time in range and time above range, along with participant acceptability of the revised treatment approach.
CONCLUSION: This study will provide prospective evidence on whether a revised hypoglycaemia treatment approach can safely reduce the glucose threshold for treatment in children and young adults using AID systems. Findings may inform future recommendations for hypoglycaemia management in the era of diabetes technologies.

articles.title: Impact of acute hyperglycaemia on cognitive function in people with diabetes: A systematic review.
articles.abstract:
AIMS: While the effect of short-term hypoglycaemia on cognitive function has been widely studied, the impact of acute hyperglycaemia on cognitive performance in people with diabetes is poorly understood. This systematic review summarised evidence on the effect of acute hyperglycaemia on cognitive functioning.
METHODS: Searches were conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO from conception to 5th March 2025. People with type 1 diabetes (T1D), type 2 diabetes (T2D) or control participants were included. Studies with the main outcome of dementia were excluded. A narrative synthesis was undertaken.
RESULTS: Eighteen studies were included, involving children and adults with T1D and T2D, using observational and experimental designs. Findings were synthesised by cognitive function domain: attention, processing speed, executive functioning, working memory and study design. Two studies measured driving performance. At blood glucose of 10-15 mmol/L the effects were mixed. At a blood glucose of 15-18 mmol/L impairment was more consistent. Driving performance in young adults with T1D was impaired at >16.7 mmol/L. At glucose ≥20 mmol/L, most studies reported widespread cognitive impairment in especially working memory, attention and processing speed.
CONCLUSIONS: Acute hyperglycaemia impairs cognitive functioning in people living with diabetes, with effects generally increasing at higher glucose levels. Whilst this pattern was not uniform across all blood glucose ranges and cognitive domains, impairment in cognitive function could impact on everyday activities for adults and children, including schoolwork, driving and work productivity. Future research should focus on crossover or clamp studies to clarify thresholds and evaluate real-world outcomes.

articles.title: Intranasal dexmedetomidine sedation in pediatric electroencephalography: dose optimization, safety, and EEG characteristics.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of intranasal dexmedetomidine (DEX) for sedation during pediatric EEG and to explore whether EEG spectral characteristics under DEX differ from those under chloral hydrate.
METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, 224 children (0-18 years) who underwent EEG under intranasal DEX sedation at a single tertiary center (January 2024-April 2025) were analyzed. Patients were stratified into weight-based dosing (Group 1, <50 kg; median 2 μg/kg) and fixed dosing (Group 2, ≥50 kg; median 100 μg). Sedation success, onset time, total sedation time, and adverse events were assessed. In a within-subject subgroup of 11 patients with a prior chloral hydrate EEG, relative power spectral density (rPSD) in the delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands during N1 and N2 sleep was compared using patient-level paired analyses, with mean paired differences, 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and correction for multiple comparisons.
RESULTS: Initial sedation success was 94.6% in Group 1 and 94.7% in Group 2; all patients achieved adequate sedation after rescue dosing. Median onset time was 10 minutes in both groups. Adverse events were mild and self-limited (3.2% and 2.6%). No statistically significant differences in rPSD between DEX and chloral hydrate were detected in either sleep stage after correction for multiple comparisons; however, the CIs were wide, and equivalence could not be established. Interictal epileptiform discharges were visually unchanged.
CONCLUSION: Intranasal DEX is an effective, well-tolerated sedative for pediatric EEG, and a weight-stratified dosing strategy appears practical. In a small paired subgroup, no significant spectral differences from chloral hydrate were detected; these preliminary quantitative findings warrant confirmation in larger studies.

articles.title: The relationship between socio-environmental factors, brain growth and cognition in middle childhood.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The relationship between socio-environmental factors, brain growth, and cognition in childhood is unknown. This study aimed to characterize associations between (i) regional brain growth from birth to 6-8 years and socio-environmental factors; and (ii) regional brain growth and cognitive outcomes in middle childhood.
METHODS: One hundred and thirty-seven 6-8-year-old children (25 with congenital heart disease) underwent neonatal and paediatric brain MRI and a full-scale IQ assessment. Data on household income, maternal education, neighborhood deprivation, and early cognitively stimulating home environment were collected. Regional brain growth (extracerebral CSF, ventricles, cortical grey matter, white matter, deep grey matter, cerebellum, brainstem) from the neonatal period to 6-8 years was assessed using Gaussian process regression.
RESULTS: Low household income was associated with reduced cortical grey matter growth (B, 95% CI -1.14, -1.88 to -0.396; pFWE = 0.044) and extracerebral CSF expansion (-1.55, -2.51 to -0.585; pFWE = 0.042). Higher cortical grey matter (3.89, 1.12-6.65; pFWE = 0.038) and brainstem (3.24, 0.894-5.58; pFWE = 0.038) growth were associated with better full-scale IQ. Brainstem (p = 0.014), but not cortical grey matter (p = 0.177), remained significant after adjustment for socio-environmental factors.
CONCLUSIONS: Support for financially vulnerable families may promote brain growth. Brainstem growth is a brain correlate of childhood cognition independent of the effects of socio-environmental factors.
IMPACT: One hundred and thirty-seven children (25 with congenital heart disease) underwent neuroimaging at birth and at 6-8 years and a full-scale IQ assessment at 6-8 years. Household income, maternal education, neighborhood deprivation and early home environment data were collected. After adjustment for other socio-environmental factors and group, low household income was associated with reduced cortical grey matter growth and extracerebral CSF expansion. Higher cortical grey matter and brainstem growth were associated with higher full-scale IQ in middle childhood. Household poverty was linked to reduced brain growth, while cortical grey matter and brainstem growth were associated with cognitive abilities in childhood.

articles.title: Tangeretin improves Neuro-2a cell survival after oxygen-glucose deprivation via phosphorylation of Akt.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypoxic-ischemic brain injury (HIBI) results from insufficient cerebral blood flow and hypoxia and can cause severe damage to the neonatal brain, leading to long term neurological disabilities. In this study, we hypothesized that tangeretin would improve cell survival by modulating mitochondrial potential in Neuro-2a (N2a) cells after oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) via Akt phosphorylation.
METHODS: N2a cells underwent 3 hours of OGD to mimic HIBI in vitro. Cells were treated with Tangeretin +/- MK2206 (an Akt inhibitor) or vehicle immediately after OGD. Cell survival was quantified by alamarBlue, propidium iodide, and TUNEL assays. Mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) was determined by JC-1 fluorescence. Protein expression was evaluated using western blotting.
RESULTS: Treatment with tangeretin significantly improved N2a cell survival after OGD, which was reversed with co-treatment with MK2206. Specifically, tangeretin improved apoptotic DNA fragmentation in cells as measured by TUNEL assay, which was also attenuated by MK2206. OGD significantly increased the percentage mitochondrial depolarization and reactive oxygen species in N2a cells compared with normoxic groups. Tangeretin treatment significantly diminished this effect.
CONCLUSION: Tangeretin provided neuroprotection against OGD in N2a cells by enhancing cell survival, maintaining mitochondrial membrane potential and suppressing apoptosis. Tangeretin deserves further exploration for its neuroprotective effects against HIBI.
IMPACT: In Neuro-2a cells injured by oxygen and glucose deprivation (OGD), tangeretin enhances cell survival. Tangeretin-associated cell survival is mediated in part by reduced DNA fragmentation. Tangeretin preserves mitochondrial membrane potential after OGD. The neuroprotective effects of tangeretin are at least partially mediated by Akt phosphorylation. Tangeretin deserves further evaluation for its neuroprotective effects after hypoxic-ischemic brain injury.

articles.title: Risk factors for congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) are a leading cause of pediatric renal failure. This study evaluated risk factors and assessed their robustness.
METHODS: PubMed, EMBASE, and Scopus searches yielded 33 studies (24 case-control, 9 cohort). Frequentist and Bayesian random-effects meta-analyses estimated associations between CAKUT and maternal/neonatal risks.
RESULTS: Frequentist analysis identified increased risk for pre-pregnancy BMI 25.0-29.9 (OR, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.06-1.45), ≥30 (OR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.07-1.51), and ≥25 kg/m² (OR, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.11-1.37). Maternal age <20 years was protective (OR, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.51-0.73). Other predictors included family history of CAKUT/kidney disease, maternal diabetes subtypes (type 1, type 2, pre-gestational, and gestational diabetes), preterm birth (OR, 1.59; 95% CI, 1.25-2.03), small-for-gestational-age (SGA), and large-for-gestational-age (LGA). Bayesian analysis validated most factors. Although 95% CrIs crossed unity for BMI 25.0-29.9 kg/m², BMI ≥ 30 kg/m², T2DM, SGA, LGA, alcohol consumption, RASi use, and hypertension, their posterior distributions were predominantly above 1. High BMI, family history, and diabetes remained robust in high-quality subsets.
CONCLUSIONS: Confirming established risks and identifying novel associations, these findings identify maternal metabolic factors as consistent correlates of CAKUT and support their evaluation as potentially modifiable targets.
IMPACT: Current meta-analyses lack synthesis on novel CAKUT determinants (maternal exposures, comorbidities, gestational weight gain, extreme fetal weight) and Bayesian approaches, which are essential to robustly address heterogeneity in sparse data. Our frequentist analysis confirmed established risks and identified novel associations: family history, SGA, LGA, and type 1 and 2 diabetes. Bayesian meta-analysis supported the main findings and showed posterior probabilities that OR > 1 of ≥90% for BMI subgroups, T2DM, RASi use, and hypertension. Maternal metabolic factors are consistently associated with CAKUT and represent potentially modifiable targets that warrant evaluation in future prospective and interventional studies.

articles.title: Identification of associative factors for recurrent respiratory tract infection using machine learning models in preschoolers.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Childhood recurrent respiratory tract infection (RRTI) poses a significant global public health burden. This study aimed to identify factors associated with RRTI in preschool children using machine learning (ML) and to develop a web-based tool for estimating individualized RRTI probabilities.
METHODS: Two cross-sectional surveys using stratified cluster sampling were conducted in 2020 and 2025. RRTI was diagnosed according to the national criteria issued by the Chinese Medical Association and China Association of Chinese Medicine. Questionnaire data covering demographic characteristics, fetal/neonatal history, and lifestyle factors were collected.
RESULTS: Total 15,075 eligible records from two surveys were included, reporting an RRTI prevalence of 14.55%. Ten ML models were trained on 29 candidate variables. The eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model outperformed the others, yielding an area under the curve of 0.733. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis identified sleep duration, child's age, and screen duration as the top three associative variables for childhood RRTI. Forward feature selection was applied to derive a parsimonious nine-variable predictive set, which was subsequently deployed as an online application ( https://cipchina.streamlit.app/ ).
CONCLUSIONS: In a large, population-based cohort of preschool children, three factors (sleep duration, child's age, and screen duration) associated with RRTI were consistently identified across multiple high-performing ML models.
IMPACT: This study identified key lifestyle-related factors associated with recurrent respiratory tract infection in preschool children. Ten machine learning models were applied to analyze 29 variables from 15,075 Chinese preschoolers, with further importance interpreted via the SHapley Additive exPlanations. Sleep duration emerged as the primary lifestyle-related factor associated with childhood recurrent respiratory tract infection, followed by child's age and screen duration.

articles.title: Automating the Pediatric Index of Mortality 3 in the Electronic Health Record: Automated Risk Scoring Using Structured Clinical Documentation.
articles.abstract: Background The Pediatric Index of Mortality 3 (PIM3) is a validated severity-of-illness score widely used for risk adjustment, benchmarking, quality improvement initiatives, and research in pediatric intensive care units (PICUs). Its use in electronic workflows is limited by required variables that rely on clinical judgement and are traditionally abstracted manually from narrative documentation. Objectives To design, implement, and evaluate an automated PIM3 calculation within the electronic health record (EHR) using structured clinical documentation to capture non-discrete variables, and to assess clinician adoption, documentation accuracy, and concordance with manual abstraction. Methods A structured documentation template with standardized response options was developed to capture non-discrete PIM3 variables, including ventilation status, elective admission status, procedural recovery, and diagnosis category. These clinician-entered data were mapped to discrete structured data elements and combined with physiologic and laboratory inputs for automated score calculation. Documentation completion and accuracy were evaluated over a 12-month period. Automated scores were validated against manually abstracted gold standard PIM3 scores in a convenience sample of 20 targeted encounters. Results Among 923 PICU encounters, clinician compliance with structured PIM3 documentation was 95% (n=877). Of the completed entries, 84% (n=773) contained no documentation errors. Identified errors were primarily related to binary clinical judgements rather than diagnostic clarification. Of the 20 encounter validation sample, automated PIM3 scores and associated probabilities of death demonstrated near-complete concordance with manually calculated gold standard values, with no clinically meaningful discrepancies. Conclusion Automated PIM3 calculation using structured clinical documentation within the EHR is feasible and reliable for supporting standardized data capture and timely availability of risk-adjustment information. This approach reduces reliance on manual abstraction and provides a scalable informatics framework for quality improvement, benchmarking, and research in pediatric critical care.

articles.title: Adversarial Safety Evaluation of a Parent-Facing, EHR-Integrated Chatbot in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit: A Red-Teaming Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Red-teaming (adversarial safety testing) of family-facing clinical chatbots remains limited.
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to red-team a parent-facing, EHR-integrated pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) chatbot.
METHODS: We evaluated 120 chatbot responses across 10 synthetic patients and six adversarial attack vectors (realistic parental challenges) with two conversational turns. Two PICU physicians independently scored each response as pass or fail against vector-specific safety criteria, classified failures by type, and rated response quality (1-5) and harm severity (0-5). Each failure involving a false parental assertion was posed again as a neutral factual query to distinguish uncritical deference from retrieval failure. As a proof of concept, all failures were retested with a modified system prompt requiring verification of parent-stated facts.
RESULTS: The pass rate was 86.7% (104/120; 95% CI: 79.3-92.2%). Pass rates by vector ranged from 65% (fragmented input) to 100% (emergency triage). Of 16 failures, 10 (63%) accepted false parental assertions; 9 of these appeared to reflect uncritical deference rather than data retrieval failure. Twelve failures (75%) carried no or negligible potential harm; two were minor, two serious, and none were catastrophic. The modified prompt resolved 12/16 failures (75%).
CONCLUSION: The dominant failure mode was uncritical acceptance of false parental assertions despite access to correct EHR data, and fragmented input posed a greater challenge than overt adversarial pressure. A targeted prompt-level mitigation resolved most failures in proof-of-concept testing. For family-facing clinical AI, helpfulness must not override fidelity to the medical record; further evaluation with real families and multi-turn testing is needed.

articles.title: Consensus Statements on the Clinical Practice for Patients With Fontan-Associated Liver Disease.
articles.abstract: The Fontan procedure has been transformative for patients with univentricular physiology. By using a single ventricle as the systemic pump and relying on passive venous return to drive pulmonary circulation, Fontan circulation alleviates cyanosis and heart failure, allowing children to engage in normal activities during school and adolescence. Nevertheless, Fontan circulation is characterized by chronically elevated systemic venous pressure, which leads to systemic venous congestion and long-term multiorgan effects. Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD) is now recognized as a major long-term complication. Approximately 50% of patients develop hepatic abnormalities within 10-20 years after surgery, and some progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Despite this risk, strategies to identify individuals at high risk for early HCC and to provide better prognostic information remain limited. This article compiles knowledge from congenital heart disease specialists and hepatologists on FALD, including areas where evidence is limited. By facilitating early diagnosis, structured follow-up, and multidisciplinary management of FALD, this initiative aims to improve outcomes, build a nationwide clinical experience, and ultimately support the development of formal, evidence-based guidelines for FALD management.

articles.title: Strengthening Rural Prevention Networks Through Government-University-Community Partnerships: Evidence from a Demonstration of a Community-Based System of Family Support for Preventing Child Welfare System Involvement.
articles.abstract: This study examines a five-year primary prevention demonstration project designed to reduce child maltreatment and family separation in an eight-county rural Midwestern U.S. region through a government-university-community partnership. By introducing four community-led capacity building strategies across the region, The Family Strong Community Collaborative sought to strengthen local family support systems and prevent the unnecessary use of foster care when child safety was not an immediate concern. Reflective inquiry revealed key organizational drivers and contextual factors for forming partnerships that provide a conceptual framework for future work. Evidence revealed that implementation drivers promoted successful collaboration and contributed to changes in the local prevention service network. Specifically, social network analyses of the local prevention service provider network revealed steady growth over time and emergence of new core members, suggesting increased capacity for coordinated service access and support. Findings suggest that systematic cross-sector collaboration supported by organizational, competency, and leadership drivers, can strengthen collaborative infrastructure and support the development of interconnected community prevention networks. While preliminary and noncausal, these findings offer a promising model for collaborative rural prevention networks and highlight strategies for building strong government-university-community partnerships that support long-term system improvement.

articles.title: Quick Parenting Assessment (QPA) Screening Tool: Helping Health Care Providers Identify Parenting Needs and Prevent Child Abuse.
articles.abstract: Harsh parenting (e.g., spanking, yelling) can negatively affect children's physical and mental health and development. The Quick Parenting Assessment (QPA) is a brief screening tool designed to facilitate provider-parent discussions about, and identification of, harsh parenting behaviors. The QPA assesses prior month use (yes/no) of seven types of child discipline behaviors: five punitive (spanking, yelling, threatening, shaming, and time-out) and two positive (redirecting and setting expectations). This study assessed the QPA's psychometric properties and clinically meaningful scoring. Participants were female primary caregivers (N = 333) recruited from WIC clinics in the greater New Orleans, Louisiana area, with an index child mean age of 8 years (SD = 1.3). Validity, reliability, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were conducted. Construct validity was assessed using parenting measures including the Attitudes Toward Spanking scale (ATS), use of spanking, and the Parenting and Family Adjustment Scale (PAFAS), which included both coercive and positive parenting practices. Criterion validity was assessed using child behavior measures including the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) and the Child Adjustment and Parent Efficacy Scale (CAPES). ROC analyses used a CBCL score > 60, an accepted cutoff for identifying clinical risk. The QPA showed acceptable internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.71) and modest test-retest reliability (r = 0.67). Strong construct validity was demonstrated with higher QPA scores correlated with higher use of spanking (r =  .53, p <  .001), coercive parenting (r = 0.50, p <  .001), and support for spanking (r = 0.43, p <  .001), and less use of positive parenting strategies (r =  - 0.41, p <  .001). Criterion validity was also supported as higher QPA scores were correlated with more child behavioral problems (r = 0.20 to 0.27, all ps <  .01). QPA item-level correlations with parenting and child measures were strongest and most highly significant for spanking, yelling, and threatening. ROC analyses indicated that a QPA (two-caregiver version) score greater than 4 yielded sensitivity of .60, and a QPA (single-caregiver version) score greater than 3 yielded sensitivity of .70. Sensitivity improved (.88-.89) when flags were based on these cutoff scores or endorsement of any one of these items: spanking, yelling, and threatening. These findings both affirm and expand knowledge of the QPA's psychometric strengths and provide more nuanced guidance for child health and family service professionals using this screening tool for both primary and secondary prevention of child abuse, thereby improving child health outcomes.

articles.title: Drug Development in Pediatric Heart Failure: Current Landscape and Future Directions.
articles.abstract: Pediatric heart failure (HF) remains an important area of unmet medical need. Pharmacological treatments primarily consist of adult drugs used off label in children. HF regulatory guidance specific to pediatric drug development is limited. The diversity in underlying pathophysiology necessitates a shift toward a mechanism-of-action driven approach. We examine the current landscape of pediatric HF, identify key challenges and opportunities for drug development, and discuss a paradigm shift to a new high-level HF phenotype classification system for pediatric HF. Pediatric extrapolation utilizing pharmacokinetics and bridging biomarkers, especially given the absence of validated surrogate endpoints, remains a promising strategy for subsets of pediatric HF physiology. Ongoing reorganization of pediatric regulatory frameworks presents a key opportunity to promote harmonization between pediatric requirements from regulatory agencies across jurisdictions. We describe innovation in pediatric HF treatment through use of extrapolation, bridging biomarkers, and adaptive trial design.

articles.title: Predicting mortality in pediatric cases with severe traumatic brain injury: is the Eppendorf-Cologne Scale more reliable than Glasgow Coma Scale?
authors: TraumaRegister DGU® of the German Trauma Society (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Unfallchirurgie; DGU)
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) in children is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, requiring reliable tools for early assessment and prognosis. While the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is the standard neurological evaluation tool, it has limitations in pediatric patients. The Eppendorf-Cologne Scale (ECS), originally developed for adults, emphasizes pupil size, reactivity, and motor response and may offer advantages in children.
METHODS: This multicenter cohort study analyzed TraumaRegister DGU® data from 5,851 pediatric patients (mean age 9.6 years). Documentation included prehospital and in-hospital assessments, injury characteristics, and outcomes. ECS and GCS scores were evaluated based on first recorded prehospital values. Predictive performance for mortality and severe TBI was assessed using AUROC analysis.
RESULTS: Among the cohort, 2,582 patients (44.1%) had severe TBI and 476 (8.1%) died in hospital. GCS showed slightly higher accuracy for predicting severe TBI (AUROC 0.778, 95% CI 0.766-0.791) than ECS (AUROC 0.745, 95% CI 0.731-0.758). For mortality prediction, ECS performed marginally better (AUROC 0.943, 95% CI 0.929-0.957) than GCS (AUROC 0.910, 95% CI 0.896-0.924). Mortality rates were 90% in the worst ECS category and 55% in the worst GCS category.
CONCLUSION: GCS showed higher discrimination for severe TBI, whereas ECS showed higher discrimination for in-hospital mortality among patients with severe TBI. ECS may provide complementary prognostic information, but its clinical utility and role alongside GCS require prospective evaluation.

articles.title: Teletherapy for Adolescent Mental Health: A Scoping Review of Comparative Effectiveness.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Teletherapy has become an increasingly common delivery format for adolescent mental healthcare, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. Given adolescents' distinct developmental characteristics, its effectiveness requires evaluation against in-person treatment and alternative remote formats. The objective was to map the randomized controlled trial (RCT) evidence on teletherapy for adolescent mental health and to conduct a quantitative synthesis where the evidence permits.
METHODS: Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews guidance, six databases were searched for RCTs published from 2014 onward that evaluated therapist-delivered remote psychotherapy for adolescents (13-18 years) with diagnosed mental health conditions, compared with face-to-face treatment, an alternative teletherapy format, or a waitlist or minimal-contact control. Quantitative synthesis was stratified by comparator type.
RESULTS: Eighteen RCTs across eight diagnostic categories were included. Six compared teletherapy with face-to-face treatment, six compared two remote formats, and six used only waitlist or minimal-contact controls. Among face-to-face comparisons, two obsessive-compulsive disorder trials met noninferiority margins, two anxiety trials nonsignificantly favored face-to-face treatment (g = -0.54 and -0.45), and single tic-disorder and insomnia trials found no clear difference. Teletherapy was superior to waitlist or minimal-contact control for anxiety (k = 6, g = 1.56, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.75-2.38) and depression (k = 5, g = 1.14, 95% CI: 0.64-1.64). Risk of bias was low in 3 of 18 trials.
CONCLUSIONS: Teletherapy improves adolescent anxiety and depression relative to waitlist or minimal-contact controls, although the size of the benefit is uncertain. Face-to-face comparisons are few, and their findings differ by condition, so equivalence to in-person care cannot yet be established. Condition-specific trials with face-to-face comparators are needed.

articles.title: Ideal sleep duration as a potential explanation of the bimodal chronotype: An exploratory study.
articles.abstract: Regarding circadian typology, the existence of a fourth category, the bimodal types, was previously proposed. Bimodal types would be those answering some questions as morning types, while others as evening types, resulting in a different sleep-wake cycle compared to intermediate types. The aim of this study was to further explore the plausibility of this new circadian typology category, attempting to determine whether it qualifies as a genuinely new category of individuals or merely a byproduct of another individual difference, namely ideal sleep duration. To this end, we reanalyzed data previously collected from 1583 children and adolescents (817 females, mean age of 13.13 ± 1.96) and 2115 adults (1144 females, mean age of 44.50 ± 5.64) who completed the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire for Children and Adolescents (MEQ-CA) and the MEQ, respectively. The open-ended questions on the ideal bedtime and get-up time were used to compute the ideal total sleep time that was later grouped into three categories: short- (≤6 hours), medium- (6 < x < 12 hours), and long sleepers (≥12 hours). In children and adolescents, bimodal types were overrepresented in both short and long sleepers and underrepresented among medium sleepers; separately considering the gender variable, the same pattern of results was detected in males only. Regarding adults, an overrepresentation of bimodal types was observed among long sleepers and their underrepresentation among medium sleepers; this same distribution was replicated only in males. It seems that the suggested fourth category of circadian typology, that of bimodal types, may be considered as a byproduct of the individual difference in ideal sleep duration.

articles.title: Associations of Vaping and Smoking Expectancies and Subsequent E-cigarette Ever-Use among United States Adolescents: A Two-Year Longitudinal Cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: E-cigarettes continue to be the most common tobacco/nicotine product among United States adolescents. Understanding the predictive value of vaping and smoking expectancies can help prevent youth e-cigarette use.
METHODS: This longitudinal cohort study analyzed the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study 6.0 data to examine vaping and smoking expectancies (15-item scales ranging 1-5) for adolescents aged 12-13 years (baseline) who had never used an e-cigarette. A dual vaping-smoking expectancy variable (low vaping/low smoking, low vaping/high smoking, high vaping/low smoking, high vaping/high smoking) was created, and multivariable regressions tested the association between vaping, smoking, and dual expectancies and e-cigarette use susceptibility as well as ever-use by age 14-15 (two-year follow-up).
RESULTS: Among 1,990 participants at baseline, the mean (interquartile range) vaping and smoking expectancies were 2.3(1.8-2.8) and 1.7(1.2-2.0). Both vaping expectancy and smoking expectancy at baseline were associated with e-cigarette use susceptibility at baseline (AOR[95%CI]=3.8[2.8-5.1],p<.001; 3.1[2.2-4.2],p<.001; respectively) and subsequent ever-use at two-year follow-up (3.0[1.9-4.8, p<.001); 2.5[1.6-3.9], p<.001; respectively). Dual vaping/smoking expectancy showed a dose-response relationship with susceptibility to e-cigarette use (high/high, 8.3[5.4-12.9]p<.001; high/low, 3.9[2.3-6.8],p<.001; low/high, 2.9[1.8-4.6],p<.001 vs. low vaping/low smoking) and ever-use (6.4[2.4-17.1], p<.001; 6.1[2.0-18.7],p=0.002; 3.9[1.4-10.9], p=0.01; vs. low/low). Adolescents with high vaping and high smoking expectancies tended to be older, female, and report lower parental monitoring and school environment scores(p<0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: Vaping, smoking, and dual expectancies were associated with risk of e-cigarette use susceptibility and ever-use within two years. Identifying adolescents with high vaping and smoking expectancies offers a crucial opportunity to implement targeted interventions aimed at preventing youth vaping.

articles.title: Longitudinal trends in early childhood sleep and napping behaviors.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Although most children discontinue daytime napping by six years of age, longitudinal evidence describing how napping changes over time remains limited. We examined 6-month changes in nap duration, frequency, timing, spontaneity, and proportion of daytime sleep in preschool-aged children.
METHODS: At baseline, 702 parents representative of the Canadian population completed surveys about their children aged 1 to 6 years, inclusive. Six months later, 162 parents reported on their child's napping (duration, frequency, timing, spontaneity, and proportion of daytime sleep) and nighttime sleep (duration and sleep problems). Children were categorized at baseline into nap profiles-regular, intermittent, spontaneous, or non-nappers-and changes were examined overall and within profiles.
RESULTS: Among children napping at baseline, 25.2% had ceased napping at follow-up, whereas 11% of baseline non-nappers resumed napping. Among children napping at both time points, nap duration and proportion of daytime sleep significantly decreased over 6 months. The largest reductions in nap duration were observed among regular nappers. Nap timing and spontaneity remained relatively stable. Nighttime sleep duration did not significantly change; however, nighttime sleep problems decreased over time.
CONCLUSION: Preschool nap behaviors are dynamic and vary by nap profile. Regular nappers exhibited the most pronounced reductions, while some non-nappers resumed napping. These findings support flexible, developmentally sensitive definitions of nap cessation and highlight the importance of individualized approaches to supporting sleep during early childhood.
CURRENT KNOWLEDGE/STUDY RATIONALE: Most research on preschool napping has focused on single sleep measures and has provided limited longitudinal evidence on how multiple nap behaviors change over time. This study examined 6-month changes in several dimensions of napping among children classified into distinct nap behavior profiles.
STUDY IMPACT: Preschool nap behaviors changed differently across nap profiles, with regular nappers showing the largest reductions in daytime sleep and some non-nappers resuming napping. These findings suggest that nap cessation is a dynamic process and support flexible, individualized approaches to defining and managing daytime sleep in early childhood.

articles.title: Histologic Patterns That Hinder Detection of Cirrhosis on Routine Abdominal Imaging: Steatosis, Centrizonal Sinusoidal Fibrosis, and Biliary-type Cirrhosis.
articles.abstract:
CONTEXT.—: Early detection of cirrhosis is essential for guiding management and prognostic surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma. Although elastography-based techniques are increasingly used, abdominal computed tomography (CT) remains the most routinely performed imaging modality in chronic liver disease surveillance.
OBJECTIVE.—: To evaluate concordance between routine abdominal CT and histology for detection of cirrhosis and investigate potential drivers of discordance.
DESIGN.—: Surgical liver pathology specimens (2018-2019) with corresponding abdominal CT within 90 days were included. Radiology and pathology reports were analyzed for the presence or absence of cirrhosis; discordant cases underwent double-blinded rereview by subspecialists. Pathology rereview assessed fibrosis stage, pattern, and quality (progressive versus regressive; Beijing classification), as well as with secondary histologic findings.
RESULTS.—: Initial concordance for cirrhosis/no cirrhosis was 88.7% (754 of 850). Rereview improved concordance to 95.8% (786 of 820), with 3 "Rad-overcalls" and 17 "Rad-undercalls" corrected by radiology. Persistent "Rad-overcalls" (n = 17) were explained by reclassified pathology (n = 12; 70.5%) or centrizonal sinusoidal fibrosis (n = 4; 23.5%). Among 29 persistent "Rad-undercalls," underlying etiologies included steatotic liver disease (n = 7; 24.2%), biliary atresia (n = 4; 13.7%), active hepatitis (n = 3; 10.3%), primary sclerosing cholangitis (n = 2; 7%), and primary biliary cholangitis (n = 1; 3.5%). All discordant pediatric cases (n = 4) had biliary cirrhosis unrecognized on CT. Discordance was significantly higher in biliary cirrhosis from biliary atresia (100%) versus primary sclerosing cholangitis or primary biliary cholangitis (12.5% each; P < .001).
CONCLUSIONS.—: Routine abdominal CT demonstrates high concordance with histology for detection of cirrhosis. Discordance arises mainly from centrizonal sinusoidal fibrosis, biliary atresia, and steatotic liver disease, underscoring limitations of CT in these settings.

articles.title: National survey of the clinical profile and management of patients with hereditary angioedema due to C1-inhibitor deficiency in Colombia.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is a rare, often misdiagnosed disorder. Epidemiological data on this condition are scarce in Latin America, particularly in Colombia. This study aimed to describe the demographics, clinical features, and treatment of Colombian HAE patients in order to address data gaps.
METHODS: A web-based survey (Sept, 2021-Mar, 2023) of Colombian physicians managing HAE patients collected anonymous data on demographics, clinical features, and treatments. Statistical analyses compared patients receiving long-term prophylaxis (LTP) versus those who did not.
RESULTS: The survey included 42 physicians from 19 Colombian provinces, covering 274 HAE patients. Median age at symptom onset was 13 years, with a diagnostic delay of 8 years. Most patients were female (59.85%) and had a family history of HAE (83.58%). Attacks mainly affected peripheral, abdominal, and facial areas; common triggers included stress, trauma, and menstruation. Hospitalization was reported by 46.24% of patients, with 23.77% hospitalized in the preceding year and 4.96% requiring intubation. All received on-demand therapy, mainly icatibant (91.41%). Long-term prophylaxis was prescribed in 52.14% of cases, with danazol (66.67%), tranexamic acid (31.21%), and lanadelumab (17.02%). These patients had longer diagnostic delays and higher hospitalization rates compared to those not receiving prophylaxis (p < 0.01 and p = 0.01, respectively).
CONCLUSIONS: This study shows significant diagnostic delays and treatment challenges for HAE in Colombia. Underreporting and geographic disparities suggest an underestimated prevalence. The findings underscore the urgent need for greater awareness, equitable access to therapies, and robust patient registries in order to address unmet needs and reduce the burden of HAE for affected individuals.

articles.title: Goat milk infant formula and gut health: from traditional nutrition to scientific innovation.
articles.abstract: When breastfeeding is not possible, goat milk-based infant formula (GMF) provides an alternative to cow's milk-based formula. This narrative review evaluates clinical, observational, and mechanistic evidence on the nutritional suitability of GMF and its potential relevance to infant gut health. Randomized trials and meta-analytic evidence support the safety and nutritional adequacy of GMF. Its distinct composition, including a higher β-casein-to-αs1-casein ratio and differences in the profile and concentrations of oligosaccharides and bioactive proteins compared with cow's milk, provides biological plausibility for differences in curd formation, protein digestion kinetics, and microbial fermentation. However, these mechanistic findings do not establish clinical benefit. Controlled evidence does not currently demonstrate that GMF prevents or treats feeding-related gastrointestinal symptoms, including infant colic and functional constipation, although observational studies suggest possible symptom differences in some infants. Well-designed randomized trials in symptomatic infants are needed to evaluate gastrointestinal outcomes, microbiota development, immune effects, and the potential value of emerging formula innovations. Future GMF development may combine the goat milk matrix with recombinant human milk proteins or microbiome-targeted ingredients to complement components that are absent, present at low concentrations, or altered during processing; however, their application and clinical benefits in GMF remain to be established.

articles.title: Overweight, obesity, and sex differences in the acquisition of aquatic motor competence among 4-5-year-old preschool children: a quasi-experimental study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Childhood overweight and obesity are associated with impaired motor competence, yet evidence on how weight status relates to structured aquatic motor skill learning in preschoolers-and whether sex moderates this relationship-remains scarce. This study compared changes in aquatic motor competence between overweight/obese and healthy-weight 4-5-year-old preschoolers following a common 8-week structured aquatic programme, and examined sex differences.
METHODS: Sixty 4-5-year-old children (30 overweight/obese, 30 healthy-weight; 15 boys and 15 girls per group) without prior systematic aquatic exposure were recruited from two kindergartens in Taiyuan, China. Weight status was classified using the Chinese Growth Standard for Children Under 7 Years (WS/T 423-2022) and WHO criteria. All children completed a 16-session, 8-week structured aquatic motor skill programme (45 min/session, 2 sessions/week, 1:5 instructor-to-child ratio). Aquatic motor competence was assessed pre- and post-intervention using the Actual Aquatic Skills Test (AAST; 17 items, range 17-51). The primary analysis examined differential change over time using a 2 (Group) × 2 (Sex) × 2 (Time) mixed-design ANOVA; estimated mean differences are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and effect sizes as Cohen's d and partial η 2. A 2 × 2 factorial ANOVA on post-intervention scores was retained as a secondary analysis.
RESULTS: Pre-intervention AAST scores did not differ between weight-status groups (t = -0.76, p = 0.448) or between boys and girls (t = -0.94, p = 0.353). The Group×Time interaction was significant (F(1,58) = 31.88, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.355): healthy-weight children showed greater mean improvement than overweight/obese children (mean Δ 27.50 vs. 23.40 points; mean difference 4.10, 95% CI 2.65-5.55; Cohen's d = 1.46, 95% CI 0.89-2.03). The Sex×Time interaction was also significant (F(1,58) = 5.15, p = 0.027, partial η 2 = 0.082): girls showed greater mean improvement than boys (mean Δ 26.43 vs. 24.47; mean difference 1.96, 95% CI 0.23-3.70; Cohen's d = 0.59, 95% CI 0.07-1.11). The Group×Sex interaction on post-intervention scores was not significant (F(1,56) = 0.22, p = 0.645, partial η 2 = 0.004; interaction contrast on change scores 0.34 points, 95% CI -1.10 to 1.78).
CONCLUSION: In this convenience sample of Chinese preschoolers, healthy-weight children and girls showed greater mean improvement in aquatic motor competence than overweight/obese children and boys, respectively, following a common structured aquatic programme. Because the design lacked a non-intervention control group, these findings are associative and do not establish that weight status caused the differential response. Longer and more individualised aquatic curricula, potentially combined with nutritional and psychological support, warrant prospective evaluation in randomised trials for overweight/obese preschoolers.

articles.title: Construction of a nomogram prediction model for symptom residue after tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy in children with obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome based on lasso-logistic regression analysis.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To identify the factors associated with residual symptoms after adenotonsillectomy in children with obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) using LASSO-logistic regression, and to construct a nomogram prediction model.
METHODS: A total of 324 children with OSAHS treated at our hospital from January 2023 to March 2024 were enrolled and randomly divided into a training cohort (n = 227) and an internal validation cohort (n = 97) at a ratio of 7:3. According to the 1-year follow-up results, the training cohort was further divided into a recovery group and a residual symptom group. In addition, 175 children with OSAHS treated at our hospital from April 2024 to January 2025 were included as an external validation cohort. LASSO-logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of postoperative residual symptoms. A nomogram model was then established and evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA).
RESULTS: Compared with the recovery group, children in the residual symptom group were younger and had higher proportions of males, BMI > the 95th percentile, family history of OSAHS, asthma, rhinitis, >8 spontaneous awakenings per hour before surgery, AHI > 18 events/h before surgery, as well as higher preoperative mYPAS scores and postoperative Wong-Baker scores (all P < 0.05). LASSO-logistic regression identified sex, BMI, asthma, rhinitis, number of spontaneous awakenings before surgery, and preoperative AHI as independent predictors (all P < 0.05). The AUC values of the nomogram in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts were 0.874, 0.851, and 0.850, respectively. Calibration curves showed good agreement between predicted and observed outcomes, and DCA demonstrated favorable clinical utility.
CONCLUSION: The nomogram showed good predictive performance and may help assess the risk of residual symptoms after adenotonsillectomy in children with OSAHS.

articles.title: When kidneys fail again: management of kidney allograft failure in children.
articles.abstract: Many children who receive a kidney transplant will require more than one transplant during their lifetime. When the first graft fails, decisions made during this transition may affect not only the return to kidney replacement therapy but also the chances of receiving a subsequent transplant. In particular, withdrawal of immunosuppression, development of HLA sensitization, graft intolerance, and the decision to remove or retain the failed allograft require careful consideration. In this Mini Review, we examine the epidemiology and causes of kidney allograft failure in children and discuss the practical challenges that follow graft failure. Evidence specific to children is scarce, especially regarding how and when immunosuppression should be withdrawn. Current data favor early preparation for retransplantation and avoidance of unnecessary sensitization. An asymptomatic failed allograft can generally remain in situ, whereas nephrectomy is reserved for specific indications. Despite greater sensitization after a first transplant, second kidney transplants in children can achieve good graft survival. Prospective pediatric studies are needed to determine how immunosuppression and the failed allograft should best be managed while preserving access to retransplantation.

articles.title: Could excessive infant mattress firmness contribute to positional plagiocephaly in Japan? An international comparison and hypothesis paper.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: International infant sleep-surface standards primarily address the prevention of overly soft sleep surfaces using pass/fail test methods rather than specifying a directly comparable consumer firmness value in Newtons. No international standard establishes an upper firmness limit for infant mattresses. Japan has no infant-specific national mattress firmness standard.
OBJECTIVE: To document the firmness (Newton value, N) of Japanese commercially available infant mattresses, compare these values against international regulatory frameworks and selected manufacturer recommendations, and propose a biomechanical hypothesis suggesting that excessive mattress firmness may contribute to the apparently higher prevalence of positional plagiocephaly (PP) reported in Japanese cohorts.
METHODS: Firmness values (N; JIS K6400-2 Method A, 40% compression) were collected from publicly available manufacturer or retailer specifications for ten Japanese infant mattress products satisfying pre-defined inclusion criteria (the primary analysis dataset). Two additional products, identified outside the original search during revision, are reported as a sensitivity check only. International reference values were obtained from regulatory documents, selected European manufacturer guidance, and product documentation. PP prevalence data were extracted from peer-reviewed literature; cross-national comparisons are presented as illustrative only.
RESULTS: Japanese infant mattress firmness ranged from 160 to 285 N (median 183 N, ten-product primary analysis). No direct numerical comparison with European density-based manufacturer recommendations is made, as no validated conversion between density (kg/m3) and ILD firmness (N) exists. Five products had firmness at or below 176 N; four products exceeded 190 N. Of the ten products, six fell within the Korean reference-test-mattress specification range (170 ± 20 N = 150-190 N), indicating that the Japanese market does not consist uniformly of extreme outliers. This preliminary survey is restricted to ten products identified through publicly accessible manufacturer or retailer specifications; independent laboratory verification was not performed.
SAFETY STATEMENT: Existing evidence strongly supports firm sleep surfaces as a key measure for reducing sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) risk. The present hypothesis concerns only the upper end of the firmness spectrum-specifically, whether surfaces that are excessively firm may carry biomechanical consequences distinct from those of appropriately firm surfaces. This paper does not recommend using softer mattresses, adding comfort toppers, or using positioning pillows or positioners.
HYPOTHESIS: Excessive mattress firmness may reduce occipital contact surface area (increasing interfacial pressure: P = F/A) and may reduce small spontaneous head-position changes during sleep (a direction that remains to be tested), thereby increasing sustained focal pressure on the immature, malleable calvaria and potentially contributing to the apparently higher PP prevalence reported in Japan.
CONCLUSIONS: Japanese infant mattresses surveyed had a median firmness of 183 N. Among the regulatory frameworks reviewed, Japan lacks an infant-specific national mattress firmness standard, and no international standard establishes an upper firmness limit. Independent market-wide testing and prospective outcome studies are warranted to determine whether an infant-specific upper firmness range should be considered.

articles.title: Exploring and interpreting how nurses experience and attribute meaning during pediatric emergencies.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Appropriate and adequate use of clinical tools is important for achieving positive outcomes in patients during emergencies. This can be achieved when tools are understood based on their mode of Being and spatial value to Dasein rather being understood by the characteristics and properties they possess. However, there is little empirical research on how nurses deal with and encounter these tools, their lived experience of these tools, and their meaning-making of these tools in pediatric emergency care.
PURPOSE: This study aimed to explore and interpret how nurses experience and make meaning of the "mode-of-Being" and use of clinical tools in emergency pediatric care within the context of their everyday clinical practice.
METHODS: A phenomenological design was adopted to explore tool use among pediatric emergency nurses in a hospital emergency ward. Qualitative data were collected through interviews and analyzed using Diekelman-Allan-Tanner's method.
FINDINGS: Team application of the A, B, C, D, E (airway, breathing, circulation, dehydration, and exposure to trauma) protocol optimizes pediatric emergency care; work fashion as an ecosystem; human, institutional, and financial constraints; and three team-pillar approaches to professional development.
PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS: This study will benefit children undergoing emergency treatment and enhance both experiential and theoretical knowledge of tools by nurses, thereby resulting in effective and efficient use of tools and higher-quality care outcomes.

articles.title: Language outcomes in preschool children with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy treated with therapeutic hypothermia.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To investigate language outcomes in preschool children with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) treated with therapeutic hypothermia and without major neurodevelopmental disabilities, and to identify early developmental and neonatal factors associated with language disorder at preschool age (LD).
METHODS: This prospective longitudinal cohort study included children with moderate-to-severe HIE treated with therapeutic hypothermia at a tertiary neonatal center and followed through preschool age. Children with cerebral palsy, intellectual disability (IQ <70), autism spectrum disorder, major genetic disorders, severe global developmental impairment, or other neurological conditions precluding reliable formal language assessment were excluded. Early developmental functioning was evaluated using the Griffiths Mental Development Scales at 24 months. Language skills were assessed between 30 and 76 months of age using standardized age-appropriate Italian instruments, and LD was identified on the basis of standardized assessment combined with clinical evaluation. Neonatal variables included cord blood pH, base excess, cerebral function monitoring, and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
RESULTS: Seventy-five children completed language assessment. Nineteen children (25.3%) met criteria for LD. Difficulties were more frequent in expressive language domains, with naming deficits observed in 62.7% and articulation/repetition difficulties in 61.3% of participants. Children who subsequently developed LD had significantly lower Griffiths Hearing and Speech (Scale C) scores at 24 months compared with children without LD [median 75 [IQR 67-80] vs. 88 [81-95], p < 0.001].
